sens: Act of mocking someone, openly ridiculing them
Words or gestures of derision directed at a person
Suffering endured due to being mocked or humiliated
G1701.detail:
1. Mockery is the act of mocking someone, turning them into a subject of ridicule — it is an act of hostility or contempt expressed openly. It humiliates the one who suffers it by belittling or dishonoring them.
2. It manifests through words or gestures of derision: insults, sarcastic laughter, grimaces, humiliating gestures. It is a form of verbal or physical aggression directed straight at someone.
3. In Hebrews 11:36, the word refers to the suffering that the faithful of the Lord endured when they were mocked: "others suffered mockings and scourging, chains and imprisonment." Mockery is listed among the persecutions and tortures inflicted on believers.
G1701.origine: The Greek word empaigmos comes from the verb empaidzô (to mock, to ridicule) and the root paix (to play, to joke). It is a noun that denotes the action or result of this ridicule. The word belongs to the same family as "empaidzô," which is found in the Gospels when soldiers mock Jesus. In Hebrew, the same concept is expressed by terms like "qalasah" (mockery, derision).
G1701.emploi: The word empaigmos appears only once in the New Testament, in Hebrews 11:36, where it is included in a list of persecutions suffered by the saints of the Old Testament. It is listed alongside scourging, chains, and imprisonment — concrete and very real sufferings. Mockery there takes on a character of persecution, not trivial or benign, but serious and painful, worthy of being mentioned alongside physical tortures. It illustrates how the faithful were treated with contempt and humiliation for their faith.
G1701.portee: This word reminds Christians that ridicule and mockery are a form of persecution. By listing mockery among the great sufferings endured by ancient believers, the epistle to the Hebrews takes it seriously — it is no less real than chains or imprisonment. For the Christian reader exposed to derision because of their faith, this word affirms that their suffering is known and honored by God.

sens: To make fun of someone, to turn them into a subject of derision
To ridicule someone in words or gestures
To deceive or trick someone
G1702.detail:
1. To mock someone is to turn them into a subject of ridicule, to openly deride them. This is what the Roman soldiers do to Jesus in Matthew 27:29: they crown him with thorns and mock him by calling him "King of the Jews." The chief priests do the same at the foot of the cross (Matthew 27:41). It is a mockery that combines words and gestures.
2. The word can also refer to the act of ridiculing someone with hurtful words, without necessarily involving gestures. The men who guard Jesus mock and strike him (Luke 22:63). A man who begins to build a house may be mocked if he cannot finish it (Luke 14:29).
3. Finally, empaizō can mean to deceive or trick someone: Herod believes he has been deceived, "played" by the Magi who do not report back to him about the child (Matthew 2:16). The word here evokes the idea of being fooled, of being the object of a deception.
G1702.origine: The Greek word empaizō is composed of em- (in, into) and paizō (to play, to act like a child). The basic image is that of play, but a play that mocks: to play *with* someone in order to mock them, treating them as a toy. In Hebrew, this word often translates עָלַל (âlal, to do harm) or שָׂחַק (sâhaq, to laugh at, to mock). The word family includes paideia (education, educational play) and paignion (play).
G1702.emploi: The verb empaizō appears 13 times in the Gospels, always to describe a cruel and humiliating mockery. It is widely used in the Passion narrative: soldiers mock Jesus (Matthew 27:29, Mark 15:20), religious leaders mock him on the cross (Matthew 27:41, Mark 15:31), and the men who guard him mock and strike him (Luke 22:63). Outside of the Passion, the verb also appears in parables or teachings: the man who begins a house without being able to finish it will be mocked (Luke 14:29), or to express Herod's deception by the Magi (Matthew 2:16). The meaning always remains pejorative: it is a mockery mixed with contempt or violence.
G1702.portee: The repetition of the verb empaizō in the Passion reveals the systematic humiliation of Jesus: it is not an isolated mockery, but a cascade of ridicule and deception. For the disciple, this word reminds us that Jesus accepted this ignominy out of love. It also invites the believer to consider whether they themselves participate in the mockery of Christ, or if they are ready to share in his disgrace.

sens: one who mocks, who derides with scorn
one who walks, who acts according to their own desires without respecting God
G1703.detail:
1. The mocker is a person who ridicules, who turns into a subject of derision. In 2 Peter 3:3, the apostle warns that "mockers" will come in the last days, bringing their ridicule. This is someone who refuses to take seriously, who delights in ridiculing.
2. The mocker is also characterized by their behavior: they "walk according to their own lusts," meaning they act without restraint, guided solely by their desires. In Jude 1:18, these mockers are described as "walking according to their ungodly lusts" — they live according to their carnal passions, despising the order that God has established.
G1703.origine: The word comes from the verb "empaïzo" (to mock, to deride) formed from "païzo" which means to play. The mocker is therefore one who "plays against" someone, who makes them the object of their malicious play. It is an active term: it is not someone who laughs passively, but someone who acts to ridicule, to hurt through derision.
G1703.emploi: The word appears twice in the New Testament, in both places where the end times are discussed. In 2 Peter 3:3 and Jude 1:18, the same warning recurs: mockers will arise, characterized by their ridicule and their carnal life. These mockers do not simply hold false opinions; they actively propagate them by ridiculing those who believe. They embody an attitude of rebellion: they refuse apostolic teaching and live "according to their lusts," indifferent to God's warnings.
G1703.portee: The portrait of the mocker warns the believer of a subtle spiritual danger. It is not only one who openly fights against faith, but one who discredits it through ridicule and irony. Recognizing the mocker helps to remain vigilant: not to be disarmed by sarcasm nor led into a life dominated by carnal desires. It is a call to firmness and moral clarity in the last days.

sens: To move by walking in the midst of a group of people
To circulate, go back and forth in a place or among people
Figuratively: to be present, to dwell, to live in the midst of
G1704.detail:
1. The word describes the action of walking, moving on foot, but with the idea of going back and forth, circulating among people or in a place. It is a movement that is not static, an active presence. In 2 Corinthians 6:16, Paul quotes God's promise: "I will walk among them," which means that God will circulate, be active, and present among His people.
2. The prefix "among" (περι-) reinforces the idea of presence at the heart of a group: one does not simply pass through, one inhabits the place, one is an actor in it. God does not merely pass by; He remains and acts in the midst of His people.
3. In a figurative and spiritual sense, "to walk among" evokes a living relationship: God commits to live in constant communion with those who receive Him as a temple, sharing in their daily lives, accompanying them.
G1704.origine: The word is composed of three parts: ἐν (in), περι (around, among), and πατέω (to walk, to tread). Together, it literally means "to walk in and among." This expression translates into Greek a typically Hebrew idea: that of the active presence of God who "goes and comes" (Hebrew: halak, frequently found in the Old Testament) in the midst of His people. The Septuagint (Greek translation of the Old Testament) uses this verb to render passages like Leviticus 26:12, where God promises His walking among Israel.
G1704.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Corinthians 6:16. Paul uses it to express God's promise to be present among His church (viewed as a living temple). He recalls a word from the Old Testament, particularly Leviticus 26:12, where God commits to circulate, to walk among His people as a sign of blessing and covenant. The rare use of this term underscores its theological importance: it expresses not a distant or abstract presence, but an active and constant proximity.
G1704.portee: This word reminds Christians that God's presence is not distant or theoretical. God does not remain only "above" the heavens: He affirms His desire to "walk among" those who receive Him as Lord, participating concretely in their lives. It is a call to live one's faith as a living communion with the God who is present, active, and near.

sens: To completely fill someone's stomach by feeding them to the point of fullness
To fully satisfy a deep desire or need
To fill the heart or soul with an emotion, a joy
G1705.detail:
1. To satisfy means to feed someone until they are no longer hungry. It is the image of a stomach filled to the brim. Luke reports that God "has filled the hungry with good things" (Luke 1:53): He has fed those who have lost everything. After the multiplication of the loaves, when the crowds "were satisfied," Jesus asks to gather the leftovers (John 6:12) — the meal was so abundant that no one suffers from hunger anymore.
2. By extension, the word also means to satisfy an inner desire or need. Paul writes that he hopes to be "satisfied" with his desire to visit the Romans (Romans 15:24): his heart will be at peace when this wish is fulfilled.
3. To satisfy can also mean to fill someone with joy or intense emotion. God "fills" hearts with joy (Acts 14:17) — He pours out such abundant joy that it overflows. It is a filling from within, not just of the belly.
G1705.origine: The word is composed of the prefix ἐμ- ("in," "inside") and a root meaning "to fill." In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, it translates notably the verb מָלֵא (maléa), which means "to fill" or "to be full." The word evokes the image of a container filled to the brim, or of a need that is completely satisfied. The primary root is that of the verb "to fill," but the prefix ἐμ- intensifies the meaning: it is about filling not halfway, but completely.
G1705.emploi: This verb appears 5 times in the New Testament Greek, mainly in the Gospels and the epistles. Luke uses it twice to describe physical fullness: God satisfies the hungry (Luke 1:53) and Jesus multiplies the bread until the crowds are satisfied (John 6:12). The opposite idea appears in Luke 6:25: "Woe to you who are full" — the rich who enjoy comfort here will suffer deprivation at judgment. Acts 14:17 broadens the meaning: God "fills" hearts with joy, showing that the word applies to emotional or spiritual satisfaction. Finally, Romans 15:24 uses the past participle in the sense of being "satisfied" with a desire. The verb thus oscillates between physical satisfaction and the satisfaction of the heart.
G1705.portee: This word reminds us that deep satisfaction comes from God alone. The hungry whom God satisfies are not only fed but honored — God overturns the order of the world by filling the poor and sending the rich away empty (Luke 1:53). For Christians, to satisfy also speaks of the joy and peace that only Christ can give to the heart: a joy that completely fills, not a superficial pleasure. It is an invitation not to seek satisfaction in the riches or pleasures of the world, but in communion with God.

sens: To physically fall into a place or a pit
To be a victim of something, to be struck by misfortune
To succumb to temptation or guilt
To incur judgment or condemnation
To fall into someone's hands
To be engulfed in ruin
G1706.detail:
1. The primary sense is literal: to fall into a hole, a pit. Jesus speaks of a sheep that "falls into a pit" on the Sabbath (Matthew 12:11): it is a concrete fall from which the owner must pull it out. The same image appears in the parable of the blind man: "Will they not both fall into a pit?" (Luke 6:39) — a real fall in the literal sense.
2. To be a victim of misfortune or aggression: the traveler in the parable "fell among robbers" (Luke 10:36) — not that he physically fell, but that he found himself in the hands of criminals, a victim of fate.
3. To succumb to guilt or sin: a newly converted bishop must not "fall under the judgment of the devil" (1 Timothy 3:6) — to be defeated by pride and fall under spiritual condemnation.
4. To incur dishonor and disgrace: a bishop must have a good reputation "so that he does not fall into disgrace" (1 Timothy 3:7) — that is, to lose his honor and be trapped by the devil.
5. To be engulfed: those who desire to be rich "fall into temptation, into a snare, and into many desires" (1 Timothy 6:9), then "plunge men into ruin."
G1706.origine: The verb ἐμπίπτω is composed of ἐν ("in") and πίπτω ("to fall"). The image is that of falling inward: not just to fall, but to fall into something, to be engulfed. In Hebrew, the verb נָפַל ("to fall") expresses both physical falling and defeat or death. This Greek composition retains this versatility: a fall that carries the one who falls to the bottom of that into which they collapse.
G1706.emploi: This verb appears seven times in the New Testament, especially in Luke and in Paul's epistles. In Luke, the usage often remains concrete and narrative: the sheep, the blind man, the assaulted traveler (Matthew 12:11; Luke 6:39; 10:36). In Paul, particularly in 1 Timothy, the meaning becomes spiritual and cautionary: one "falls" under judgment, into disgrace, temptation, or a snare. Only once, in Hebrews 10:31, does the eschatological image appear: "to fall into the hands of the living God" — to be thrown into the hands of the one who judges. The context changes the meaning, but the idea of sinking, victimization, and loss of balance remains.
G1706.portee: This word reminds Christians that spiritual falling is not abstract: it is like a pit, a trap, into which one sinks. Paul's warnings to church leaders (1 Timothy 3:6-7) teach that vigilance, humility, and good reputation preserve from guilt and judgment. For those who suffer from desire or temptation, this term shows that these things are not fleeting temptations: they risk engulfing us, losing us. Conversely, the image of the sheep that the shepherd pulls out of the pit speaks of the grace that lifts us up.

sens: To weave together, intertwine (primary sense)
To engage in something that holds back, distracts
To be caught by, to be overcome by something
G1707.detail:
1. The word primarily evokes the action of weaving or intertwining threads together — this is the first image of the Greek verb. Although this literal meaning does not appear in our New Testament, it illuminates all the others.
2. Figuratively, it means to be entangled with something, that is, to engage in affairs that hold us back and distract us from what truly matters. A soldier must not be entangled in civilian affairs if he wants to please the one who enlisted him (2 Timothy 2:4): he would then be attached, held by a thousand threads.
3. The verb can also mean to be caught, to be overcome by something — like someone who has been ensnared in nets. Those who have escaped the corruption of the world through Jesus Christ but become entangled again are overcome by that corruption (2 Peter 2:20).
G1707.origine: The word is composed of the prefix ἐν (en) and the verb πλέκω (to weave, to braid). The image is of something that intertwines, wraps around oneself. The simple verb πλέκω appears in the New Testament to describe the weaving of the crown of thorns (Matthew 27:29). Our word adds the idea that what intertwines holds us, embraces us.
G1707.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the New Testament, both in the passive voice (that is, in the form 'to be entangled' or 'to be overcome'). In 2 Timothy 2:4, Paul uses it to urge young Timothy not to be held back by civilian affairs when serving God. In 2 Peter 2:20, Peter describes the tragic fate of those who, having known Jesus Christ, return to the corruption of the world: they become captives of it. The context in both cases is that of spiritual warfare and faithfulness.
G1707.portee: This verb invites the Christian to examine what holds them back and distracts them from their commitment to God. It serves as a reminder that it is possible to become ensnared, entangled by the concerns of the world or by returning to old sins. It is a gentle but firm warning: Christian freedom is fragile and requires vigilance.

sens: The action of braiding hair, intertwining it into braids or elaborate ornaments
Body ornamentation through sophisticated hairstyles
G1708.detail:
1. Braiding hair is the action of intertwining hair to form braids or complex arrangements. It is a meticulous manual task that requires time and attention. Peter refers to it in 1 Peter 3:3 as a form of 'external adornment.'

2. More broadly, this word denotes a type of adornment, a form of beautification of the body through hairstyle: that is, the overall ornament created by the elaborate braiding of hair. It was a common practice among wealthy women who sought to display themselves through their outward appearance.
G1708.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb meaning 'to intertwine' or 'to weave together' (en- + braid). It literally evokes the gesture of passing hair between each other to form an intertwined pattern. The same family of words in Greek describes the action of weaving fabrics and braiding ropes: what matters is the work of intertwining. This vocabulary of braiding applies to concrete material domains — hairstyling, weaving, equipment.
G1708.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Peter 3:3. Peter uses it to describe a form of external adornment for women — the elaborate braiding of hair — which he classifies among superficial ornaments (along with gold and expensive clothing). In this context, Peter does not condemn hairstyling itself, but warns against the tendency to seek one's value and beauty in crafted physical appearance rather than in the inner and lasting beauty of the heart.
G1708.portee: This passage invites the believer to reconsider the importance they place on their outward appearance and material adornments. It is a call to cultivate the beauty of the soul — gentleness, patience, kindness — rather than investing time and resources solely in seduction through physical appearance. For those seeking to follow Christ authentically, this word reminds us that true beauty is not in what is seen, but in what endures.

sens: To blow on something or someone
To breathe, to be alive
Figuratively: to exhale, to show outwardly
G1709.detail: 1. The primary meaning is literal: to blow or breathe on someone. It is the gesture of bringing air or life through breath. 2. The word also simply means to breathe, that is, to live and have breath. 3. Figuratively, the Bible uses it to describe what a person exhales, what they manifest through their behavior: thus Saul 'breathed threats and murder' (Acts 9:1) means that violence and hatred emanated from him, filling his entire attitude.
G1709.origine: The word comes from two Greek elements: 'en' (within) and 'pnéō' (to breathe, to blow). It is the same root that gives us the French 'pneuma' (breath, spirit). The Hebrew word נְשָׁמָה (néshama), which means the vital breath or breath, is close in meaning. The composition with 'en' suggests the idea of bringing in or manifesting through breath.
G1709.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament according to the provided usages: in Acts 9:1. Paul uses this vivid image to show how Saul, before his conversion, was filled with rage against Christians — he 'breathed' literally threats and murder, as if these violences were coming out of him with every breath. It is a dramatic way to describe not only his actions but his inner state and the passion that drove him. The Old Testament also uses it to speak of the breath of life or being alive.
G1709.portee: This verse reminds us that our words, actions, and attitudes reflect what truly fills our hearts. Before his encounter with the Lord, Saul 'breathed' threats and murder — this showed the depth of his hatred. For the Christian reader, it is an invitation to examine what we 'breathe': our habitual thoughts, our dominant emotions, and especially the fruit of the Spirit that we allow to flow within us.

sens: to travel for commerce
to exchange goods for profit
to exploit someone for gain
G1710.detail:
1. The word primarily describes the action of traveling, particularly for the purpose of doing business and buying or selling goods. In James 4:13, merchants say 'we will go to such a city' to 'trade': they are planning a lucrative business trip.
2. More broadly, to trade means to do business, to exchange goods or services for money, with a view to personal profit. It is the normal activity of a merchant or trader.
3. The word takes on a pejorative nuance when it comes to exploiting or deceiving someone for advantage. In 2 Peter 2:3, false teachers 'will exploit you' with deceptive words: they will use you, manipulate you, to enrich themselves at your expense.
G1710.origine: The word comes from the family of ἔμπορος (emporros), which means merchant or trader. The root ἔμ- (em-, 'in') combines with πορ- (poreuomai, 'to go, to travel'), painting the image of a person who 'goes along the roads' to buy and sell. In Hebrew, we find a similar idea with סָחַר (sahar), which denotes trade and commerce.
G1710.emploi: The verb appears twice in French in the New Testament. In James 4:13, businessmen speak of their plans for a commercial trip with confidence, without recognizing God's sovereignty: they decide to 'trade' and gain. In 2 Peter 2:3, the same verb is applied to false teachers who exploit Christian disciples through deception and misleading words to enrich themselves. The word thus shifts from the neutral idea of commerce to a morally reprehensible activity: to take advantage of others dishonestly.
G1710.portee: This word reminds the Christian of the dangers of the love of money and the exploitation of others. In James, it invites trust in God rather than in our carnal plans. In 2 Peter, it warns against those who exploit faith for gain, calling the reader to vigilance and discernment against false teachers.

sens: Commercial activity, exchange of goods
Business, trade that yields profit
Worldly occupations that distract from what truly matters
G1711.detail:
1. Traffic is the activity of one who buys and sells goods for profit: it is commerce in the broad sense. In the parable of the wedding feast (Matthew 22:5), a guest neglects the royal invitation to attend to his traffic, showing the importance he places on his business affairs.
2. By extension, the word refers to business and trade in general — everything that occupies a businessman concerned with his gain. It is a legitimate activity in itself, but it can become an all-consuming concern.
3. Figuratively, traffic symbolizes worldly occupations, earthly concerns that capture attention and divert from spiritual priorities. In the context of Jesus, refusing the divine call for one's traffic means choosing visible riches over the kingdom of God.
G1711.origine: The Greek word emporia comes from emporos, "merchant" or "trader" — literally one who travels from port to port to sell. It thus designates the characteristic activity of the merchant: buying here, selling there, always in motion for profit. In biblical Hebrew, this word primarily translates sachar ("to trade") and rakhal ("to be a merchant"), verbs that also evoke this circulation of goods and the pursuit of gain.
G1711.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Matthew 22:5, in the parable of the king who prepares a feast for his son. The guests refuse to come: one goes to his field, the other to his traffic. The context shows that traffic is among the earthly concerns that cause neglect of the call of the kingdom of heaven. It is not that commerce is bad in itself, but it represents here what completely occupies a man and blinds him to what truly matters.
G1711.portee: This parable challenges the believer about his priorities: where does he place his energy and desire? Traffic symbolizes any occupation, however respectable, that becomes an excuse to ignore God's call. It is an invitation to examine whether our business, our occupations, our material concerns are gradually distancing us from communion with God and His kingdom.

sens: place of exchange and commerce
lucrative commercial activity
G1712.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a place where commercial exchanges take place, a market where one buys and sells. In John 2:16, Jesus sees the temple in Jerusalem transformed into a "house of traffic": merchants sell animals for sacrifices and exchange money, reducing the holy place to a mere marketplace.
2. By extension, it describes the activity itself: commerce, lucrative business. It is less about the physical place than the spirit of profit and trade that drives those who operate in this place. Jesus refuses to allow the house of prayer to become the seat of mercantile activity.
G1712.origine: The Greek word comes from "emporios" (merchant, trader). It is a concrete noun formed from the root that expresses the idea of crossing, passing through — the merchant "crosses" places to sell. The same Greek word translates in ancient Greek the Hebrew "sakan" (traffic, trade) and "rakal" (to do business). The central idea is that of an activity of exchange and commerce.
G1712.emploi: The word appears only once in the Greek New Testament, in John 2:16, during the cleansing of the temple. It is Jesus Himself who uses it to denounce the profanation of the holy place. The context is specific: the temple had become not just a place of exchange, but a house of traffic, where profit took precedence over reverence. This passage reveals Jesus' thoughts on the sacred and the profane, on what has no place in the house of God.
G1712.portee: This word reminds believers of the necessity to preserve the sacred from the profane, and the importance of the purity of worship. It invites examination of how one enters into the presence of God: with a heart seeking commercial exchange or in true worship? The denunciation of traffic prompts each Christian to ask whether their spiritual motivations are authentic or have become mercantile.

sens: One who buys and sells goods for profit
Person engaged in traveling commerce
Figure of one who seeks or invests in something of value
G1713.detail:
1. The merchant is a trader who buys and resells goods to make a living and become wealthy. This is his profession: he travels roads and seas to find products, sell them elsewhere, and make a profit. In Revelation 18:3, the merchants of the earth have grown rich through the luxury of Babylon, as they have sold their goods there.
2. Etymologically, the Greek word first evokes a traveler, someone who undertakes a commercial journey to trade. It is a traveling merchant or maritime trader who does not stay in one place but constantly moves for business.
3. Jesus uses the image of the merchant to speak of one who seeks and invests in what truly has value. In Matthew 13:45, the merchant seeking fine pearls represents the seeker who recognizes the value of the Kingdom and dedicates all he possesses to it.
G1713.origine: The Greek word ἔμπορος comes from πόρος (poros), which means "journey" or "passage." Thus, etymologically, it is one who makes journeys, a traveler. The Hebrew סָחַר (sachar) and רָכַל (rakal), which this term generally translates, also designate the trafficker or one who negotiates, emphasizing exchange and profit.
G1713.emploi: The word appears five times, always in the New Testament: once in Matthew in the parable of the Kingdom, and four times in the description of the fall of Babylon in Revelation 18. In Matthew, it is a positive image: the merchant of pearls symbolizes one who discovers the supreme value of the Kingdom and renounces everything for it. In Revelation, it is a dark image: the merchants are presented as actors in the economic and spiritual corruption of Babylon, enriched by its luxury and immorality. Their mourning at the fall of Babylon shows that their wealth was based on immorality.
G1713.portee: This word of Jesus invites the reader to ask: what am I really investing to obtain the Kingdom? The merchant of pearls abandons all he possesses when he discovers the object of supreme value. In contrast, Revelation warns against wealth based on compromise with evil: the merchants of Babylon illustrate how the thirst for profit can chain one to an ungodly system and lead to ruin.

sens: To set on fire, to destroy by fire
To be inflamed, to become ardent (fig.: irritation, anger)
G1714.detail:
1. This verb primarily means to destroy something by subjecting it to flames. It is a destructive and violent act: in Matthew 22:7, the king orders the city of the murderers to be burned, a classic biblical image of judgment. The fire symbolizes divine or royal anger that annihilates what opposes it.
2. In a figurative or passive sense, the word can evoke the burning of the body or heart: to be inflamed with fury, indignation. It is this fervor, this inner inflammation, that causes one to act violently.
G1714.origine: The verb comes from a Greek root (πίμπρημι: pimprēmi) that means "to make burn, to inflame." The prefix ἐμ (em) intensifies the action. In the Old Testament, this word often translates the Hebrew verb שָׂרַף (sāraph), which has the same meaning: to burn, to consume by fire. The common idea is that of complete and irreversible destruction by flames.
G1714.emploi: This verb appears very rarely in the New Testament (only once in Matthew 22:7 in the parable of the wedding feast of the king's son). It fits into a context of divine judgment: the king sends his armies to kill the assassins and burn their city in vengeance for his outrage. It is a verb of violence and punishment, used to depict royal or divine anger.
G1714.portee: This word reminds us that divine judgment is not a theological abstraction, but a terrible reality that destroys evil at its root. For the disciple listening to Jesus tell this parable, the "burning" of the city evokes the end times and the fate of those who reject the Lord's invitation. It is a sober and grave warning about the consequences of sin and the refusal of God.

sens: Forward, face to face with someone or something
In the presence of, under the eyes of
At the front, in first position
In regard to, in the eyes of (figurative sense)
G1715.detail:
1. Before describes a concrete spatial position: being face to someone, in front of them. When a man with dropsy stands "before" Jesus (Luke 14:2), he is physically in His presence, visible and close. This is the opposite of being behind or hidden.

2. The word also means to be "under the eyes of" someone, in their presence, which creates a relationship of visibility and often of judgment. When Jesus is brought "before" Pilate (Matthew 27:11), He appears face to face with the governor. Galatians 2:14 shows Paul speaking to Cephas "in the presence of all," meaning publicly, before witnesses.

3. Before can also express an advance, a priority: John the Baptist says that another came "before" him, meaning he preceded him in dignity and authority (John 3:28).

4. In a moral or spiritual sense, before designates what is manifested "in the eyes of" God or men. When one gives alms "before" men (Matthew 6:1), one acts visibly; when one confesses Jesus "before" God the Father (Matthew 10:32), it is with full awareness, before the supreme judge.
G1715.origine: The Greek word ἔμπροσθεν (emprosthen) is formed from ἐν (en, in) and πρόσθεν (prosthеn, the front). It literally describes what is "toward the front." The root πρόσ- appears in other words expressing the front or priority. In Hebrew, the word עֳנִי (poor) in the Old Testament is not directly related; rather, Greek uses before to translate the notion of being "face to" someone in a context of judgment or appearance.
G1715.emploi: This word appears about 47 times in the New Testament, mainly in Matthew, Luke, and John. It first functions as a spatial adverb: "to be before," "to put before." Then it becomes a preposition: "before someone." Its usage varies according to context: in judgment scenes (Matthew 27:11, Luke 21:36, 2 Corinthians 5:10), it expresses appearance; in faith scenes, it emphasizes public testimony (Matthew 10:32, Luke 12:8) or the manifestation of glory (Matthew 17:2, Mark 9:2); in the epistles, it indicates conscious presence before God (1 Thessalonians 1:3, 3:13). The meaning evolves from spatial (physical position) to spiritual and judicial (presence before the judge).
G1715.portee: For the Christian reader, "before" reminds us that nothing is hidden: our actions, our words, our confessions are always done "before" someone — men or God. This awareness of divine presence invites honesty and sincerity. Confessing Jesus "before" men engages our public responsibility; our works shine "before" them and glorify God. It is also a word of judgment: we will all appear "before" the judgment seat of Christ (2 Corinthians 5:10), hence the importance of living in the awareness of this eternal presence.

sens: To project saliva onto someone or something, out of contempt or disgust
To insult, humiliate someone with this gesture
G1716.detail:
1. The word designates the physical act of spitting: projecting saliva from the lips. It is a concrete, brutal gesture. In the Passion narratives, Roman soldiers literally spit on Jesus: "they spat on him" (Matthew 27:30), or "spat on him" after striking him (Mark 15:19). This detail shows the humiliation of Christ's body.
2. Beyond the physical gesture, to spit expresses extreme contempt, a voluntary humiliation. This is why this verb is often accompanied by other insults: one spits on him "while covering his face and striking him with fists" (Mark 14:65). Spitting becomes a symbol of total hatred and rejection, which explains why it is part of the sufferings of the Passion foretold in advance: "they will mock him, they will insult him, they will spit on him" (Luke 18:32).
G1716.origine: The Greek word ἐμπτύω (emptuō) is formed from the prefix ἐν (en-, in) and πτύω (ptuō, to spit). It expresses an action directed toward someone: to spit *on* or *against*. It is a simple verb, whose physical meaning is primary and constant. In the Greek Old Testament, it corresponds to the Hebrew יָרָק (yaraḳ, to spit).
G1716.emploi: The verb appears 6 times in the New Testament, only in the Passion narratives (Matthew, Mark, Luke). Matthew places it during the judgment before the Sanhedrin (26:67) and during the mockery of the soldiers (27:30). Mark mentions it three times: in Jesus' prophecy to his disciples (10:34), then during the interrogation of the Sanhedrin (14:65) and during the mockery of the soldiers (15:19). Luke includes it in Jesus' prediction (18:32). Each time, it is an act of derision, insult, and contempt toward Jesus, integrated into the series of violence and humiliations he endures.
G1716.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader of the extent of Jesus' sufferings, not only physical but also moral and spiritual. To spit on someone is one of the worst insults: it is to deny human dignity even to one who is rejected. Jesus accepted this extreme humiliation for us. By meditating on this detail, the Christian sees that Christ bore the weight of men's contempt, assuming our guilt and our shame.

sens: Visible, apparent, that which shows clearly
Made visible, brought to light
Revealed, publicly known
G1717.detail:
1. The word describes what is visible and apparent, what imposes itself on the sight without ambiguity. In Acts 10:40, when Peter says that God "allowed him [Jesus] to appear," the word emphasizes that the resurrection was not hidden or doubtful: it was shown clearly and manifestly to the witnesses.
2. It can also express the idea of making visible, bringing to light what was hidden. It is the action of producing or revealing something publicly.
3. In Romans 10:20, Paul quotes Isaiah: "I was manifest to those who did not ask for me." Here, God reveals His presence and love to people who were not even seeking Him — He makes Himself visible and known in an unexpected and free manner.
G1717.origine: The word comes from the verb "to show in" or "to exhibit" (formed from the prefix "in" and the verb "to show"). It belongs to the family of Greek words expressing visibility and manifestation. This term often translates into Greek the Hebrew ideas of "being established" or "being known" — the idea that something becomes visible and recognizable to all.
G1717.emploi: The word appears twice in the New Testament translated by the Segond. In Acts 10:40, Peter asserts that the resurrection of Jesus was manifested — made visible and certain — to the apostles and disciples. In Romans 10:20, Paul borrows the words of the prophet Isaiah to show that God voluntarily revealed Himself to pagan nations who were not seeking Him. In both cases, the word emphasizes the public, clear, and undeniable nature of this revelation.
G1717.portee: This word reminds us that the resurrection of Jesus is not a vague spiritual intuition, but a fact made visible and manifest. It also tells us that God does not hide from sincere seekers: He makes Himself known, even to those who do not expect Him. For the Christian, this affirms that faith rests on a visible and tangible reality, and that God takes the initiative to reveal Himself.

sens: To appear, to show oneself visibly to someone
To manifest, to reveal one's presence
To declare, to inform, to communicate information
To file a complaint, to make an accusation
G1718.detail:
1. To appear, to show oneself visibly to someone: the word primarily denotes the act of becoming visible, of manifesting oneself to the eyes of a person. After his resurrection, Jesus "appeared" to many people in Jerusalem (Matthew 27:53), and his transfigured body became visible to the saints who came out of the tombs.

2. To manifest, to reveal one's presence: this means to show who one truly is, to unveil oneself to someone with whom one enters into a relationship. Jesus promises: "I will make myself known to the one who loves me" (John 14:21-22) — he will reveal his presence and love in a personal and intimate way.

3. To declare, to inform, to communicate information: the word takes on a more administrative hue, meaning to report or expose facts to someone. The tribune "made" a report to the young man (Acts 23:22), and the Jews "filed a complaint" with the governor against Paul (Acts 24:1), that is, they presented their accusation.

4. To file a complaint, to make an accusation: when accusers come before an authority to present their grievances against someone, they "address" their complaint (Acts 23:15, 25:2) — they officially make known what they accuse the defendant of.
G1718.origine: The word combines the prefix "en" (ἐν) and "manifest, visible" (φανής, from φαίνω, to shine or appear). It literally means "to make visible, to bring to light." This verb belongs to the family of φαίνω (to appear, to shine) and φανερός (manifested, known). In Acts, where it is frequent, it takes on a legal and administrative tone, that of presenting a case before the authorities.
G1718.emploi: The verb appears ten times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospel of John and in Acts. In John 14:21-22, Jesus uses it to promote a personal and intimate revelation to his disciples who love him — this is the most spiritual meaning. In Matthew 27:53, during the resurrection, it describes the visible appearance of the resurrected saints. But in Acts (23:15, 22, 24:1, 25:2, 15), the context changes: Paul is brought to trial, and the word takes on the meaning of an administrative declaration, a complaint or an accusation presented before a magistrate. In Hebrews 9:24 and 11:14, it regains a spiritual nuance (the manifestation of Christ, the confession of one's convictions).
G1718.portee: For the believer, this word teaches that Jesus does not reveal himself to the world in general, but to those who love him and keep his commandments. It is a personal and elective relationship: God "makes himself known" to those who truly seek him. At the same time, the word reminds us that there is a visible revelation, an appearance of Christ that has already occurred and that will have a future fullness. In the life of faith, to "make oneself known" to God also means to be honest, manifest, transparent — a lesson that Acts also applies to public testimony before authorities.

sens: Filled with a sudden and deep fear
Terrified, impressed by something extraordinary or superhuman
G1719.detail:
1. The word describes a fear that suddenly seizes someone, that overwhelms them. This is the state of the women who came to Jesus' tomb on the morning of the resurrection: they are seized with fear upon seeing the empty tomb and hearing the announcement that Jesus is alive (Luke 24:5). They find no normal explanation for what they see.

2. This word also expresses respectful fear or religious awe in the face of the extraordinary. Cornelius is seized with terror upon seeing the angel of the Lord (Acts 10:4) — a fear mixed with respect. Similarly, when an earthquake destroys part of Jerusalem, the survivors are terrified and recognize the hand of God (Revelation 11:13). It is a fear that opens the eyes to the power of God.
G1719.origine: The Greek word is composed of two elements: "en" (in) and "phobus" (fear, terror). The image is that of a fear that enters you, that overwhelms you from within. The root "phobus" is the same that gives rise to the words "fear" and "dread" in French. It describes not an ordinary fear, but a deep terror that seizes you in the face of the extraordinary.
G1719.emploi: This word appears six times in the New Testament, always to describe a reaction of fear in the face of something superhuman or unexpected. The women at the tomb are seized with fear (Luke 24:5, 37). Cornelius, a high-ranking Roman centurion, is terrified by the appearance of an angel (Acts 10:4). Felix, the governor, becomes frightened when Paul speaks of the coming judgment (Acts 24:25) — his conscience is troubled by this message. Finally, when God gives a sign through an earthquake, people are terrified and recognize his power (Revelation 11:13). In all cases, it is an intense fear, often followed by the recognition of God or faith.
G1719.portee: This word shows us that fear is not inherently bad: it is the right reaction in the face of an encounter with God or the revelation of his power. The women at the tomb, Cornelius, even Felix — all are terrified, and this fear brings them face to face with the reality of God. It is an invitation not to seek to rationalize what God does, but to recognize with respect that he truly acts in this world and asks to be listened to.

sens: To direct one's breath towards someone or something
To give or communicate something through a gesture of breath
To entrust the Spirit or a spiritual power through this symbolic gesture
G1720.detail:
1. The primary meaning is physical: to direct one's breath upon someone. It is a concrete act, a gesture where air comes out of the mouth towards a person. Genesis 2:7 (mentioned in the tradition of the word) shows God blowing to animate life.
2. This gesture becomes a sign of action or transmission: to blow on someone is to pass something to them. It is an act of power, designation, or gift.
3. In John 20:22, after his resurrection, Jesus "blew" on his disciples. This gesture accompanies his words "Receive the Holy Spirit": blowing becomes the visible sign of an invisible transmission, of the Spirit of God given to the apostles for their mission.
G1720.origine: The Greek word comes from the root "physaō" which means "to blow" or "to inflate" — the image of breath escaping. The prefix "em-" (in-) indicates that the breath goes inward, that it penetrates. In Hebrew, the verb "nāphach" (נָפַח), which also means "to blow," is regularly translated by this word in the Greek Old Testament. Breath ("pneuma" in Greek, "ruach" in Hebrew) is throughout the Bible the image of life and the Spirit of God.
G1720.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in John 20:22, at the moment when the resurrected Jesus entrusts to his disciples the mission of apostles and the gift of the Spirit. The gesture of blowing echoes creation in Genesis 2:7, where God blows the breath of life into the nostrils of man. Here, Jesus makes a parallel gesture: he "blows" the Holy Spirit into the disciples to spiritually vivify them and empower them for their mission. It is a moment of great symbolic density: the physical gesture of blowing manifests the invisible spiritual gift.
G1720.portee: This word reminds the Christian that the Holy Spirit is not just an abstract doctrine, but a living, dynamic gift that animates and transforms. The gesture of Jesus' breath shows that the Spirit comes directly from the person of the risen Christ and is given for apostles on mission. For the reader, it is a strong image: to be "blown upon" by Christ is to receive life, the capacity to serve, and the divine authentication of one's vocation.

sens: Implanted, deeply rooted in the heart
Engraved, permanently inscribed in the soul
G1721.detail:
1. The word describes something that has been put in the ground and has taken root, thus holding firmly and durably. It is an agricultural image: just as a planted seed grows in the soil, the word of God takes root in the heart of the believer who receives it with gentleness (James 1:21). This image shows that the Word does not remain on the surface — it implants and becomes part of us.
2. Figuratively, "planted" means engraved, deeply anchored in the conscience and soul. What is thus rooted withstands storms and bears fruit. James uses this word to say that the word received with humility can only save our souls — it acts as a living force implanted within us.
G1721.origine: The Greek word comes from the verb "to implant, to root." It takes up the fundamental biblical image of the sower and the harvest: the word of God is compared to a living seed that, if it falls on good soil (a willing and humble heart), grows and bears fruit. This image runs throughout the Scriptures, from Psalm 1 to the parables of Christ.
G1721.emploi: The word appears only once in Greek in the New Testament, in James 1:21. The apostle uses it to describe the word of the Lord received in the heart of the Christian. The context (rejecting filthiness and rampant wickedness, receiving it with meekness) shows that this implantation is not automatic: it requires prepared soil — a purified and teachable soul. It is a call to allow the word to truly take root in our lives, rather than remaining on the surface.
G1721.portee: This word invites the believer not to remain a passive listener of the word of God, but to let it take root within them — to meditate on it, to live it, so that it truly transforms their heart and behavior. It is a promise: such a word "can save your souls." It speaks to us of the hidden, living power of the implanted Word within us.

sens: Inside a place or space
On, at, in contact with or near something
Within a group, among people
In a state, condition, or situation
By means or instrument of something
During a period of time or at the moment when
G1722.detail:
1. Marks the location where someone or something is found: "in the city" (Luke 7:37), "in the temple" (Matthew 12:5). This is the most concrete sense, that of a person enclosed or contained within a space.

2. Indicates the position on the surface or in contact with something: "in the eye" (Matthew 7:3), meaning on the eye, visible on its surface. The word describes proximity or adherence.

3. Expresses presence in the midst of a group or community: "among you" (Luke 1:1: "in us"), like someone who is part of the group and participates in communal life.

4. Describes the state or condition in which one finds oneself: "in peace" (Mark 5:25), "in glory" (Philippians 4:19), as one might say "to be angry" or "to be healthy." The word paints the overall situation in which the person lives.

5. Shows the means or tool used to accomplish an action: "by the blood" (Hebrews 9:25), "by water" (Matthew 3:11), as one baptizes someone by water or buys something with money.

6. Marks the moment or duration in time: "in three days" (Mark 15:29), "in the synagogue" in the sense of "while he teaches in" (John 6:59). It also carries the idea of "while" or "at the moment when."

7. In the Christian mystical relationship: "in Christ Jesus" (Romans 3:24, Galatians 2:17) expresses the spiritual union of the believer with Christ and their hidden life in God. This usage, typically Pauline, reveals the intimate communion that the Christian experiences with their Lord.
G1722.origine: The preposition ἐν (in) comes from classical Greek and corresponds to the Hebrew בְּ (bé) in the Greek Old Testament. It fundamentally denotes the fact of being "in" or "inside of." In classical Greek, it is used with the dative and primarily marks place or state. The New Testament extends its usage characteristically, particularly in the phrase "in Christ Jesus," which reflects the influence of Semitic thought (Hebrew also uses this preposition to express union and personal relationship). This extension creates a richness of expression: a simple preposition expresses both physical place and spiritual reality.
G1722.emploi: The word ἐν is the most frequent preposition in the New Testament, appearing over 2100 times. It appears in all the books, from Matthew to Revelation. Its meaning varies according to context. In the Gospels, it often situates the action: Jesus teaches "in" the synagogue (John 6:59), he was born "in" Bethlehem (Matthew 2:1). It also describes the internal state: sin conceived "in" the heart (Matthew 5:28). In Paul, it acquires major theological significance: "in Christ Jesus," the central phrase of his theology, denotes the new existence of the believer, saved, justified, seated "in the heavenly places in Christ" (Ephesians 1:3, 2:6). Finally, it expresses the means or instrument: to be baptized "in water" (Matthew 3:11), to be redeemed "by the blood" (Revelation 5:9). Depending on the books and usages, the word paints both geography and theology, physics and spirit.
G1722.portee: For the Christian reader, this small preposition carries immense spiritual weight. It reminds us that our faith is not a set of abstract doctrines, but a concrete and intimate relationship with Jesus Christ: "in Christ Jesus" summarizes the new life of the believer, their justification, sanctification, and future glory. It also invites reflection on the mystery of union with Christ: we are not merely "for" Christ or "after" Christ, but "in" him, like branches "in" the vine (John 15:4). This simple preposition calls the reader to deepen the idea that the Christian life is a participation in the very life of the resurrected one.

sens: To hold a child close, embracing them
To express affection or blessing through this gesture
To welcome tenderly
G1723.detail:
1. The word describes the action of taking someone in one's arms, holding them close while firmly embracing them. It is a concrete physical gesture: Jesus "took a little child, placed him in the midst of them, and took him in his arms" (Mark 9:36) to make him a living example to the disciples.
2. This gesture is never neutral: it expresses love, protection, and blessing. When Jesus "took [the children] in his arms and blessed them, laying his hands on them" (Mark 10:16), he combines affectionate embrace with the act of blessing.
3. To take someone in one's arms is also to truly welcome them, to acknowledge them, to give them value — which is what Jesus does with the little children, while the disciples wanted to push them away.
G1723.origine: The word comes from ancient Greek: the prefix "en-" (in) joins with "aggalê" which denotes arms or embrace. It is a natural and universal image: holding someone in one's arms is a gesture that transcends cultures. The ancient Greek version of the Old Testament uses this same verb to translate the Hebrew "hibbouq," which has the same meaning of embrace or hug (Proverbs 6:10; 24:33).
G1723.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the New Testament, in the two parallel passages of Mark where Jesus welcomes the children (Mark 9:36 and Mark 10:16). In both cases, this gesture accompanies his teaching on humility and receiving the kingdom of God. It is never a simple banal gesture: it is each time an act of divine tenderness, contrasting with the disciples' reflex to push the children away. The context shows that taking someone in one's arms carries a theological significance with Jesus — it is the concrete way to welcome and bless.
G1723.portee: This word shows us a Jesus who does not hesitate to physically manifest his tenderness towards the smallest and most vulnerable. It is a reminder that Christian love is not just a matter of feelings or words: it is expressed through concrete gestures, through the warmth of true presence. For the disciple, it is an invitation to welcome children and, beyond that, all those whom the world ignores or pushes away.

sens: Living creature of the sea
Being that inhabits salt water
Beast of the marine domain
G1724.detail:
1. The word refers to the creatures that populate the sea — fish, marine mammals, crustaceans, and other living beings of the ocean. In James 3:7, the apostle uses it to show that man has tamed "all kinds of beasts and birds, reptiles and marine animals": he emphasizes that even the creatures that are most elusive to us, those that live in the water far from us, remain subject to the wisdom and dominion of human beings.
2. The word encompasses everything that lives in the sea and pertains to the marine aquatic domain. It is a general category that does not distinguish between species: it simply describes the nature of the habitat — the sea — as what defines these animals.
G1724.origine: The Greek word comes from two parts: ἐν (en) meaning "in," and ἅλς (halès) meaning "the sea" or "salt," because seawater is salty. Enalios thus literally means "that which is in the sea." It is a simple and transparent compound word that primarily describes the habitat.
G1724.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in James 3:7. The apostle James uses it in his argument about human dominion over creatures: he lists four categories of animals (wild beasts, birds, reptiles, and marine creatures) to show that nothing escapes man's ability to subdue and tame creation. It is a simple and descriptive zoological term, without particular theological nuance.
G1724.portee: This passage reminds the Christian reader that God has given man a unique place: dominion over creatures. Even the most distant and inaccessible animals — those that live in the depths — are subject to human wisdom and authority. This reality speaks of the greatness of God's design for humanity and invites reflection on the responsibility that accompanies this dominion.

sens: in front of someone, in their presence
under someone's gaze, face to face
in the eyes of someone, in their judgment
G1725.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes physical position: to stand before someone, in their presence. In Luke 1:8, Zechariah performs his priestly duties "before God" in the sanctuary, meaning he is carrying out an act that takes place in divine presence, in the space consecrated for worship.
2. It then expresses the idea of being exposed to someone's gaze, being seen by them. It is a presence that engages relationship: the one who is "before" cannot hide; they are observed.
3. Finally, the word takes on a moral and spiritual significance: to be "before God" means to live under His evaluative gaze, to be judged by Him. In Acts 8:21, Simon's heart is not "right before God," meaning that God sees and judges the hidden malice in his heart — nothing escapes His discernment.
G1725.origine: The word comes from the Greek preposition "en" (in) combined with a term meaning "face to face." It is a common word in everyday Greek. The basic image is that of position: being in the "face to face" zone with someone, and then, by extension, being under their gaze and subject to their judgment.
G1725.emploi: This word appears twice in the New Testament according to our sources. In Luke 1:8, it describes Zechariah's fulfillment of his priestly service, which takes place "before God" in the sanctuary. In Acts 8:21, it characterizes the spiritual state of Simon's heart: he is not "right before God," which shows that the term extends from local meaning (position) to moral meaning (divine judgment on intentions). In both cases, "before God" emphasizes that God sees and evaluates everything that occurs in His presence.
G1725.portee: This word reminds the believer that God sees everything: not only our visible actions but also the hidden motivations of our hearts. To live "before God" is to accept being transparent before Him, to renounce pretending or hiding. It is a call to inner honesty and a devoted life that acknowledges the constant gaze of the One who knows all secrets.

sens: Face to face, in the presence of someone
Under the eyes of, visible to someone
In an opposing, hostile, or contrary manner
G1726.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes the position of one who stands in front of another, in their direct presence. When Luke says that Jesus was "a powerful prophet in deeds and words before God and before all the people" (Luke 24:19), he means that everything He accomplished and said took place under the gaze of God and the people — it was manifest, visible, in their presence.
2. The word is also used to express what is under someone's eyes, their judgment or appreciation. When God "gave Joseph favor before Pharaoh" (Acts 7:10), it means that Joseph obtained the favor and esteem of Pharaoh — he proved worthy in the eyes of the king. Similarly, when "they could not find anything to accuse in his words before the people" (Luke 20:26), it means that the adversaries found no reproach to address to Jesus' words in the eyes of the listening crowd.
3. In a more figurative sense, the word can express opposition or hostility: what is "against" someone, what is contrary or hostile to them.
G1726.origine: The Greek word ἐναντίον comes from ἀντίος, which literally means "placed in front of" or "set against." The preposition ἐν ("in") is added to reinforce the idea of position. In Hebrew, the word נֶגֶד (negued, "face to face, in front of") carries the same image: two things face to face. This root has given rise in Greek to several words of the same family expressing opposition, equality, or direct confrontation.
G1726.emploi: The word appears five times in the New Testament, notably in the Gospel of Luke and in the Acts of the Apostles, always with the meaning of "before, in the presence of." Luke regularly uses it to describe what is manifested or judged in the presence of God or a person. In Luke 1:6, Zechariah and Elizabeth are "righteous before God," meaning that their righteousness is manifest in God's eyes. In Acts 7:10 and Acts 8:32, the word retains this sense of "in the presence of," "in the eyes of." Nowhere in these usages does the word carry the hostile sense of "opposed" or "contrary," although the source definition mentions it: it is a potentiality of the word that the New Testament does not actualize.
G1726.portee: This word reveals an important spiritual reality: nothing escapes the gaze of God. What is "before God" — our actions, our words, our thoughts — exists in His presence, under His judgment. For the believer, this means that the Christian life does not play out in secret: it unfolds in the eyes of God. It is both an exhortation to sincerity and a comfort: God sees our faithfulness and our hearts.

sens: (for the wind or elements) blowing against, opposing movement
(figuratively) opposing, hostile
enemy, adversary
(in expression) in front of, before, in the presence of
G1727.detail:
1. When the disciples were rowing on the Sea of Galilee, the wind was "contrary" (Matthew 14:24, Mark 6:48): it was blowing directly against them, making navigation difficult and dangerous. The adjective describes a natural force that goes against what one wants to do.

2. Applied to people, "contrary" means hostile, opposed to someone. In Jerusalem, the Jews who persecuted Paul and the Church were "enemies" of all men (1 Thessalonians 2:15): they actively opposed the Christian faith and the people of God.

3. It is also the adversary in the sense of declared enemy. In Titus 2:8, Paul asks Christians to live healthily "so that the adversary may be ashamed": the one who accuses or fights them will have nothing to blame them for.

4. In expression ("ἐξ ἐναντίας"), the word means "in front of", "before", "in the presence of". It is an expression to indicate the place or context where something occurs.
G1727.origine: The word is formed from the root "ἀντί-" which means "in front of", "against", and the prefix "ἐν-". The primary image is spatial: two things placed face to face, in opposition. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, the equivalent word is "נֶגֶד" (negued), which literally means "face to face" or "in front of". Greek uses this same word to transition from the physical sense (opposite direction, headwind) to the moral and interpersonal sense (hostility, opposition).
G1727.emploi: The word appears eight times in the New Testament, mainly in Matthew, Mark, and Paul. Its most common usage is concrete: the three occurrences of "contrary wind" (Matthew 14:24, Mark 6:48, Acts 27:4) describe a nautical situation where the elements oppose the journey. The figurative usage (moral opposition or hostility) appears mainly in Paul: in 1 Thessalonians 2:15, the adversaries of Christ are "enemies"; in Acts 28:17, Paul defends himself against having acted "against" his people; in Titus 2:8, the adversary (probably Satan or the enemies of the Gospel) is to be ashamed. The word can also simply mean "in the presence of" or "before" without the notion of hostility.
G1727.portee: This word helps the reader recognize that opposition and hostility toward the Gospel are real: they are not imaginary, but like a headwind that truly pushes against us. For the Christian, it reminds us that obstacles—whether natural (storms), human (persecution), or spiritual (Satan)—are real and require faith and perseverance. It is also an invitation to seek the rest and presence of Jesus amid these difficulties.

sens: To undertake an action, to start it for the first time
To embark on a venture or work
To initiate a process that will continue
G1728.detail:
1. The verb expresses the action of starting, taking the first steps in something. It is simply the starting point of an action. In Galatians 3:3, Paul speaks of the moment when the Galatians "began" their Christian life by the Spirit—this beginning, this decisive first step.

2. The word also denotes commitment to a work, a direction, or a way of life that extends over time. It is less a simple moment than a sustainable initiation. In Philippians 1:6, Paul affirms that God "began" in them a "good work"—this beginning is not isolated; it involves a continuation until completion.

3. The verb carries the idea that a beginning is followed by a continuation, a progression: one "begins" something knowing or hoping that it will be pursued. This is why in Galatians 3:3 it is so absurd for Paul to start by the Spirit and end by the flesh—the logical order of the beginning should already indicate the orientation of the entire work.
G1728.origine: The Greek word is composed of "en" (in) and "archomai" (to begin, to be first). This composition reinforces the idea of initiation: it is a beginning that is *in* a process, that *enters* into action. The root also evokes the idea of "chief" or "principle" (as in "archon", magistrate). In Hebrew, this verb often translates the intensive form of the verb "halal" (חָלַל), which also carries the idea of commitment or profanation in the sense of "beginning to use"—always a transition from rest to action.
G1728.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the preserved New Testament, both times in Paul. In Galatians 3:3, he criticizes the Galatians who first received the Spirit by faith ("begun by the Spirit"), but risk ending their Christian journey by works of the law—a beginning that deviates. In Philippians 1:6, the same verb carries a promise: the work that God "has begun" in you will be brought to completion. In both cases, the beginning is never an isolated act; it carries with it a dynamic that will continue. The Pauline context thus emphasizes the coherence between the beginning and the continuation, and the decisive nature of the first step.
G1728.portee: For the Christian reader, this word invites reflection on the quality of their beginning: by what spirit did I start my new life? In Galatians 3:3, Paul warns that the spiritual beginning must orient everything else; otherwise, one goes astray. In Philippians 1:6, this word becomes a source of assurance: if God has truly begun a good work in you, do not doubt that He will bring it to completion. An authentic beginning carries within it the promise of its fulfillment.

sens: One who lacks resources to live
Destitute, lacking the essentials
Without means, in need
G1729.detail: 1. The word literally designates a person who lacks essential things—food, clothing, shelter—to survive. In Acts 4:34, the early Church in Jerusalem ensures that "there were no poor among them" by selling properties and distributing the proceeds to each according to their needs. 2. It is also a state of poverty, the material deprivation that makes a person vulnerable and dependent on the help of others. The poor has nothing to offer, nothing to give; they live in constant need. 3. The word can take on a moral dimension: one who is reduced to poverty has lost their dignity and independence, which explains why the Bible exhorts to help the poor.
G1729.origine: The Greek word comes from a root meaning "to lack", "to be deficient". It is composed of a prefix (en-) and a root that evokes emptiness, absence. In the Septuagint (the Greek version of the Old Testament), it translates the Hebrew חָסֵר (to lack) and אֶבְיוֹן (poor, one who cries out for help). The word belongs to the family of those expressing poverty and material deprivation.
G1729.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 4:34. It describes the ideal of the early Christian community in Jerusalem, where the sharing of goods is so generous that no member is left in poverty. This passage shows that the absence of the poor is the result of solidarity and the voluntary sale of properties by those who have wealth. It is a portrait of the Church living out the practical love of Jesus.
G1729.portee: This word challenges the Christian regarding their responsibility toward the poor. The ideal of the early Church—that none should be poor—is only possible through the concrete generosity of those who have wealth. It is a challenge to our personal and communal economy: are we willing to share so that no one lacks the essentials?

sens: Visible and tangible sign that manifests a hidden or affirmed reality
Clear demonstration of a truth through facts
Concrete testimony of a divine judgment
G1730.detail:
1. An evidence is a manifest sign, something that can be observed with one's eyes or heart to recognize that something is true. It is the opposite of a mere word or vague promise: it is a concrete fact that proves reality. In 2 Thessalonians 1:5, Paul speaks of the sufferings of Christians as an "evidence" of God's righteous judgment.
2. It is also the demonstration of an assertion: to show by facts that one was telling the truth. An evidence is what establishes beyond any doubt that something is true or that someone is truly acting as they say.
3. This word particularly designates a testimony or sign sent by God Himself — the way He manifests His justice or power. The sufferings endured for the Gospel thus become a visible evidence that God judges justly and that the Kingdom of God is real.
G1730.origine: The word comes from a root that means "to show" or "to manifest" (ἐν-: "in", δείκνυμι: "to show"). It is formed to designate the thing shown, the manifested reality, rather than the act of showing itself. It is a word that emphasizes the tangible and visible nature of the sign that convinces.
G1730.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Thessalonians 1:5. Paul uses it to tell Christians that their sufferings, far from being absurd, constitute an evidence — a visible and undeniable sign — of the just nature of God's judgment. These trials endured faithfully show that God truly judges and that the Kingdom they aspire to is real. This passage addresses persecuted believers, assuring them that their pains are not in vain: they manifest and attest to divine judgment.
G1730.portee: For the Christian who suffers for their faith, this word is a word of encouragement: the difficulties they endure are not a sign of God's abandonment, but rather an evidence that God judges justly and that the Kingdom of God is true. Trials become concrete signs that God has a just plan and that He will keep His promises. It is an invitation to see persecution not as a defeat, but as a visible testimony of the reality of God.

sens: To make visible or manifest, to publicly make known
To prove through demonstration or facts
To exhibit a character trait, a moral or divine quality
G1731.detail:
1. To show primarily means to make visible what was hidden or unknown. It is to exhibit, to make known in the open. In Romans 2:15, the conscience of the Gentiles "shows" that the law is written in their hearts: it makes it evident, manifest. In Ephesians 2:7, God wants to "show" in the coming ages the immeasurable riches of His grace: He would bring it to light, make it shine.

2. To show also means to prove, to establish the truth of something through concrete acts or facts. In 2 Corinthians 8:24, Paul asks the Corinthians to "show", before the churches, the proof of their charity: not just to talk about it, but to demonstrate it through actions. In Titus 2:10 and 3:2, servants and all believers must show good doctrine and great gentleness: they do this through their conduct, their visible actions.

3. To show also applies to bringing to light a quality, a feeling, a power, especially divine. In Romans 9:22, God wants to "show" His wrath and power: He manifests them through His acts. In 1 Timothy 1:16, Jesus Christ "shows" all His patience in Paul: He exhibits it, making it a living proof in him.
G1731.origine: The Greek word ἐνδείκνυμι is composed of ἐν ("in, within") and δείκνυμι ("to show"). Δείκνυμι comes from a root that means "to make see" or "to point out". The prefix ἐν reinforces the idea: to show "from within", that is, to make fully manifest. In ancient Greek, this word often translates the Hebrew לָכַד (to capture, seize) or גָּמַל (to accomplish, treat), and it evokes the idea of bringing to light, of making visible to all.
G1731.emploi: This verb appears 11 times in the New Testament. Paul uses it extensively in his letters (Romans, Corinthians, Timothy, Titus) and it is also found in the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews. The word is used to show a moral reality: the work of the law (Romans 2:15), charity (2 Corinthians 8:24, Titus 2:10), gentleness and kindness (Titus 3:2, Hebrews 6:10-11). It is also used to bring to light divine attributes: God's power and wrath (Romans 9:17, 9:22), grace and goodness (Ephesians 2:7), mercy and patience of Christ (1 Timothy 1:16). In every usage, the meaning remains: to make manifest, to prove through acts or in person.
G1731.portee: This word teaches us that authentic faith is not only expressed in words: it must be shown, proven through visible and concrete acts. Our Christian qualities — charity, gentleness, kindness — are only valuable if they are "shown", embodied in our lives. Likewise, this verb reminds us that God never hides His intentions: His justice, grace, and power are eager to be manifested in history and in our hearts. To believe is to allow God to show His splendor in us.

sens: Act of showing, making something visible
Demonstration, public manifestation
Testimony that establishes the reality or truth of something
G1732.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the action of showing, of making visible: it is to point out to say "look". In Romans 3:25-26, God "shows" His justice by highlighting the sacrifice of Christ — He makes it visible, manifest to all eyes.

2. It is then a demonstration, a solemn and public manifestation. When the Church gives "the evidence" of its charity before the Churches (2 Corinthians 8:24), it publicly exposes its fraternal love for all to see and recognize.

3. Finally, it is an evidence in the sense of what establishes the truth of something: what shows that something is real, true, certain. In Philippians 1:28, the way Christians endure persecution without fear is an evidence (an obvious sign) that God saves them — and an equally clear sign that their enemies are perishing.
G1732.origine: The word comes from the verb ἐνδείκνυμι, which means "to show, to manifest": it is composed of ἐν ("in, within") and δείκνυμι ("to show"). The basic image is therefore that of a finger pointing out, making visible what was hidden. The family of the word includes all terms related to manifestation and public exhibition.
G1732.emploi: The word appears 4 times in the New Testament, always in the writings of the Apostle Paul. In Romans 3:25-26, he describes how God "shows" His justice by justifying the believer through faith in Christ — this is the great demonstration of divine justice. In 2 Corinthians 8:24, it refers to the charity of the Corinthians that is made "visible" to other Churches: it is the living proof, the concrete attestation of their devotion. In Philippians 1:28, the firmness of Christians in the face of persecution becomes a visible evidence: for their enemies, it is the mark of their perdition; for the faithful, that of salvation. Each time, the word emphasizes what is made manifest, visible, evident to all.
G1732.portee: This word reminds us that the Christian faith is not just a matter of words: it must be shown, become visible and tangible. God's justice is proven through the work of Christ; the Church's charity is proven through actions; trust in God is proven through perseverance in trials. Each Christian is therefore a bearer of living proofs: their behavior becomes the testimony that the world sees.

sens: The number 11
The eleven apostles after Judas' betrayal
G1733.detail:
1. The word simply denotes the number 11, as a unit of count. In Greek, it is composed of "one" (hen) and "ten" (deka), forming the basis of all compound numbers between 11 and 19.
2. In the New Testament, "eleven" is almost always used to refer to the apostles after Judas' departure. When Jesus appears resurrected to his disciples (Mark 16:14), he shows himself "to the eleven" gathered at the table. After the Ascension, the group of apostles continues to be called this until Matthias is elected to replace the traitor (Acts 1:26). Peter presents himself "with the eleven" to announce Pentecost (Acts 2:14). The number 11 thus marks a time of waiting and incompleteness, between Judas' defection and the restoration of the apostolic group to its symbolically complete number.
G1733.origine: The Greek word hendeka combines the root "hen" (one) and "deka" (ten), following the model of Greek compound numbers. It is a simple numeral, without any particular theological charge originally. In Hebrew, the number eleven is expressed similarly (achad asar, literally "one ten"). The word does not carry any emotional or religious nuance in itself: it is the biblical usage that imbues it with meaning.
G1733.emploi: The word appears only 6 times in the New Testament, all in the Gospels and Acts, and always to evoke the surviving apostles after Judas' betrayal. Matthew (28:16) speaks of the "eleven disciples" in Galilee. Mark (16:14) describes Jesus appearing "to the eleven" during a meal. Luke uses the term three times in resurrection contexts (24:9, 24:33), then in Acts (1:26 and 2:14) to designate the group that welcomes Matthias and proclaims the Gospel in Jerusalem. The number 11 is never used for anything else in the New Testament: it is the specific number of the apostolic group in transition, incomplete but alive and active.
G1733.portee: This word reminds us that Judas' betrayal wounded the group of apostles, which remains marked by this absence until it is completed. It also emphasizes the continuity of testimony: despite the defection of one apostle, the others continue their mission with authority and power. For the believer, this illustrates that God does not abandon His work when His servants falter: the apostolic community rebuilds and redeploys.

sens: the ordinal number that comes after the tenth in a series
the eleventh hour of the day, in the ancient counting system
G1734.detail:
1. Eleventh simply designates the rank of an element in a sequence: after ten comes eleven. The word is an ordinal adjective, which arranges things in order. In Revelation, John enumerates the twelve foundations of the new Jerusalem by counting them one after the other: the eleventh is the jacinth stone (Revelation 21:20).
2. In the parable of the workers in the vineyard (Matthew 20:6, 9), Jesus situates a moment of the day: the eleventh hour. In Israel, hours were counted from sunrise; the eleventh hour corresponds roughly to 5 PM in the afternoon, at the end of the day. The master still recruits workers at this late hour and pays them like the others.
G1734.origine: The word comes from a root meaning the number eleven. It is a regularly formed ordinal adjective in Greek to indicate rank: just as "tenth" (second rank), "eleventh" marks the eleventh rank. It has no precise Hebrew equivalent since this technical term for ordinal numbering is specific to Greek.
G1734.emploi: The word appears only three times in the New Testament, always in an enumeration or a precise count. Twice in Matthew 20, where Jesus tells the parable of the workers hired at different hours of the day: the master recruits at the eleventh hour, that is, in the late afternoon. Once in Revelation 21, where John methodically enumerates the twelve foundations of the heavenly Jerusalem, naming the eleventh stone. The adjective is always used to count or arrange elements in an established order.
G1734.portee: This small parable of the eleventh hour teaches the sovereign grace of God: He does not judge according to the length of service or the effort made, but according to His free goodness. The last workers, hired very late, receive the same wage as the first. It is a reminder that God's generosity exceeds our human calculations.

sens: To be suitable, fitting for a situation or role
To be possible, feasible
G1735.detail:
