1. To be appropriate means to be suitable or right for someone. It indicates that something fits well with a person's function or status. In Luke 13:33, Jesus says: "It is not appropriate for a prophet to perish outside of Jerusalem" — in other words, it is not fitting for a prophet to die in exile, as Jerusalem is the place that suits his mission and dignity.
2. To be appropriate can also mean to be possible, feasible — that is, that something is within someone's reach or can be accomplished. The word expresses here the practical possibility of an action or event.
G1735.origine: The word comes from the Greek ἐν ("in", "within") and δέχομαι ("receive", "accept"). The initial image is that of "receiving within oneself" or "accepting"—hence the meaning of "to be appropriate" or "to fit". This construction expresses the idea that something fits well into a role, function, or situation: it is "received" as appropriate.
G1735.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament Greek: in Luke 13:33. Jesus uses it to affirm that it is impossible — or rather, not appropriate — for a prophet to be killed elsewhere than in Jerusalem. The context shows that Jesus is speaking of His own impending death and His dignity as a prophet. The word emphasizes that certain things align with God's will or with the nature of something, while others do not fit, even if they are technically possible. It is a theological assertion: there is an order, a fittingness in the divine plan.
G1735.portee: This word reminds Christians that God has a just and orderly plan. There is no chance in the history of salvation: Jesus' death in Jerusalem was not an accident, but something that was fitting for His mission as a prophet and Savior. This invites the reader to see beyond appearances and to recognize divine wisdom in events, even the most painful ones.

sens: To reside or dwell somewhere, to be physically present there
To stay in a given place rather than leave
To be in the presence of someone
G1736.detail:
1. The verb describes the act of living or residing in a place, like someone who usually dwells there. Here, Paul speaks of remaining "in this body" (2 Corinthians 5:6), that is, staying alive on earth with our physical envelope.
2. It also conveys the idea of staying somewhere rather than leaving: as long as we remain in the body, we are not "with the Lord" (2 Corinthians 5:8), which implies a departure, a death.
3. Finally, to remain expresses prolonged presence: this is why Paul says that we strive to please God "whether we remain in this body or whether we leave it" (2 Corinthians 5:9), showing that to remain evokes a duration, an established situation.
G1736.origine: The word comes from the ancient Greek endēmos, composed of en- ("in") and démos ("people", "place"), hence the initial image: to live among the people, to have one's dwelling there. It is the word for someone who is "at home" in a place, in contrast to someone who travels or is exiled. The root suggests a stable presence and a geographical rooting.
G1736.emploi: The verb appears only three times in the New Testament, all in 2 Corinthians 5:6-9, in a context of personal eschatology. Paul uses it to contrast two states: to remain in the physical body (on earth) or to remain with the Lord (after death and resurrection). The apostle does not use this word as a simple description of housing, but as a way of speaking about our relationship to the present incarnation and future glory.
G1736.portee: This verb helps the Christian grasp that present life is not our definitive dwelling: we are pilgrims on earth, awaiting the presence of the Lord. Paul uses it to exhort: since we only remain for a time in this body, let us strive to please God right now. It is a call to vigilance and hope.

sens: to dress someone by putting clothes on them
to wear clothes, to get dressed
G1737.detail: 1. To clothe literally means to dress someone, to put clothes on their body. In Mark 15:17, the soldiers clothe Jesus in purple: they put a robe on him to mock him. The verb expresses the action of covering the body with a garment, a piece of clothing. 2. In the middle sense (when the subject performs the action for themselves), to clothe means to get dressed, to wear clothes. In Luke 16:19, the rich man is clothed in purple and fine linen: he wears these precious fabrics that show his wealth and status.
G1737.origine: The Greek word ἐνδιδύσκω (endiduskō) is composed of the prefix ἐν- (en-, "in" or "into") and the verb δύσκω (duskō, "to enter"), which evokes the action of putting on, slipping into a garment. The root reflects the concrete image of entering into, slipping into a garment. In the Greek Old Testament, it often translates the Hebrew לָבַשׁ (lābash), which precisely means to clothe or to dress.
G1737.emploi: The verb appears twice in the New Testament according to the Segond 1910. In Mark 15:17, the soldiers "clothe" him in a mocking royal purple, a robe of derision. In Luke 16:19, it is the rich man himself who is described as "clothed" in purple and fine linen. In both contexts, the verb emphasizes clothing as an external sign: in the first case, it marks him with ridicule, in the second with wealth and prestige. The nuance between to clothe (to dress another) and to be clothed (to dress oneself) reflects the grammatical structure of the verb, which can be active or middle.
G1737.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible cares about clothing, not out of vanity but because it reveals our true values. The purple that the soldiers put on Jesus shows their mockery of the invisible King; the purple of the rich man reveals his heart attached to appearances. For the reader, to clothe invites us to ask: not only what do I wear, but who do I dress within myself through my choices and attachments.

sens: Conforming to justice, to what is right, moral and fair
Deserving to be pronounced or applied due to its conformity to justice
G1738.detail:
1. The word describes what is in accordance with justice and moral uprightness. It is the idea that something corresponds to the just order of things, to true right. In Romans 3:8, Paul asserts that the condemnation of those who slander him and claim that he encourages evil is "just": it is deserved, proportionate to their lie.
2. More specifically, it is a sentence, a judgment, a retribution that is just — that is to say, it is pronounced or applied rightly, as it corresponds to what is due. In Hebrews 2:2, the author states that every transgression has received a "just" retribution: each infraction has had its deserved and appropriate punishment.
G1738.origine: The word comes from the Greek root « δίκη » (dikè), which means "justice" or "right." « Endikos » adds the prefix « en- » (in), creating the image of what is "in the right," that is, conforming to justice. It is a relatively rare word that emphasizes the fundamentally just nature of a thing or a judgment.
G1738.emploi: The word appears only twice in the preserved New Testament, in the two given references. In both cases, it qualifies a moral or legal reality that cannot be doubted: a deserved condemnation (Romans 3:8) and a retribution proportionate to the transgression (Hebrews 2:2). The usage is always positive, in the sense that the justice in question is irreproachable. These two passages show that "just" here means a perfect conformity to what is morally and legally due.
G1738.portee: This word reminds the reader that God's justice is not arbitrary: it is "just," meaning it corresponds exactly to what must be. Whether in the condemnation of lies or in the punishment of sin, what God pronounces or allows fully deserves this name. This strengthens confidence in divine fairness and invites the believer to recognize that God's judgments are always grounded in law.

sens: The action of building, of erecting something
The constructed work, the edifice itself
Material or element that has entered into the composition of a structure
G1739.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the action of building, of erecting: it is the process by which something is constructed. In Revelation 21:18, it describes how the wall of the heavenly Jerusalem was built: it was "constructed" of jasper, meaning that jasper was part of its material composition.

2. The word can also refer to the edifice itself, the built work: it is the result of the action of building, what remains once the construction is completed.

3. In the context of Revelation, the word particularly emphasizes the material of the construction: it is not just to say "the wall is made of jasper," but to highlight that jasper has been worked, shaped, integrated into this glorious wall. It is a precious and deliberate construction.
G1739.origine: The word comes from the Greek root δωμάω (domáō), which means "to build, to erect." The prefix "en" (ἐν) reinforces the idea of construction "in" or "composing." The root itself evokes the primary image of raising a structure, of laying stone upon stone. It is a rare word in the New Testament, appearing mainly in contexts of architectural description or material composition.
G1739.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible: in Revelation 21:18. John describes the New Jerusalem with richly detailed architectural language. In speaking of the "construction" of the wall in jasper, he uses a technical term that emphasizes not only the presence of jasper but the work of building, the way this precious material has been utilized. The term emphasizes the splendor and solidity of the heavenly construction, where each element has been deliberately integrated into the whole. It is a choice of vocabulary that reinforces the magnificence of the final picture presented to John.
G1739.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that the heavenly Jerusalem is not a spiritual abstraction, but a concrete reality, beautifully built. It emphasizes that God Himself is a builder, an artisan who raises for His people a dwelling whose every stone, every material reveals His glory and wisdom. This invites contemplation of the solidity and beauty of what God prepares for those who belong to Him.

sens: To receive glory, to be rendered illustrious and honored
To be exalted, elevated in honor and dignity
To shine with splendor, to manifest one's greatness
G1740.detail: 1. The word denotes the act of receiving or obtaining glory — a renown, a splendor, a shining honor. In 2 Thessalonians 1:10, Christ will be "glorified" in His saints: He will appear in all His majesty and will be recognized, admired, celebrated by all who have believed. 2. It also conveys the idea of being elevated, exalted in dignity and power. The name of the Lord Jesus will be "glorified" in us (2 Thessalonians 1:12) when our entire life, by the grace of God, reflects His greatness and shows the world His magnificence. 3. The word finally evokes the brilliance, the splendor that shines and impresses: to be glorified is to manifest one's true glorious nature, worthy of honor and admiration.
G1740.origine: The Greek word combines the prefix "en" (in, by means of) and "doxa" (glory, splendor, honor). It comes from a root meaning to shine, to appear illustrious. In the Greek Old Testament, it often translates the Hebrew "kabach" (to be heavy, weighty, important — hence, to have weight, that is, importance and honor) or "arats" (to be terrible, impressive). These Hebrew images suggest that glory has weight, substance: it is not light or superficial.
G1740.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Greek New Testament, both in the second epistle to the Thessalonians. It is used in the passive voice (middle-passive form): it is not the subjects themselves who actively glorify, but they are glorified, exalted. In 2 Thessalonians 1:10, it is Jesus who will be glorified when He comes: His glory will become manifest and radiant in the eyes of all. In 2 Thessalonians 1:12, it is about the name of Jesus being glorified "in you" (in your lives, through your testimony) and that you be glorified "in Him" (through your union with Him): it is a mutual, reciprocal glorification, within the relationship between Christ and His people.
G1740.portee: This word reminds the believer of a central truth of his faith: the glory of Jesus Christ is not only a present and invisible reality, it will be publicly and radiantly revealed. Our calling is not only to believe, but to contribute, through our lives, to the honor and exaltation of the name of Jesus. Finally, being glorified "in Him" promises that our own life, transformed by grace, will participate in His eternal splendor.

sens: Who enjoys honor and consideration, a good reputation
Who has brilliance, splendor, magnificence
Who deserves respect and admiration
G1741.detail:
1. The word first evokes one who is held in high esteem, who possesses a good reputation and enjoys honor. It is the prestigious social status that makes one be regarded. In 1 Corinthians 4:10, Paul contrasts the Corinthians who are "honored" with himself and his companions who are "despised": to be honored is to be respected and esteemed by others.
2. The word also designates what shines with beauty, brilliance, splendor. The magnificent garments spoken of in Luke 7:25 are those that catch the eye with their richness; the glorious acts of Jesus in Luke 13:17 are those that produce admiration and joy.
3. Applied to the Church in Ephesians 5:27, the word carries a spiritual significance: the Church is "glorious" because it is made pure and without blemish, worthy of absolute respect before God. It is a moral and holy splendor.
G1741.origine: The word comes from the root δόξα (doxá), which means "glory," "honor," "brilliance." The prefix "en-" reinforces this idea: it is one who possesses glory, who is clothed in it. In Hebrew, the word it often translates is כָּבַד (kávad), which designates both honor, dignity, and the weight and importance of someone or something. Glorious, therefore, literally means "full of glory, weight, and honor."
G1741.emploi: The word appears four times in the New Testament, always to qualify what deserves esteem. In Luke, it depicts concrete realities: the sumptuous clothing of the great (7:25), the dazzling miracles of Christ (13:17). In 1 Corinthians 4:10, Paul uses it ironically to describe the social status of the Corinthians in contrast to his own contempt. In Ephesians 5:27, the meaning rises to an eschatological level: the glorious Church is the one that Christ prepares for Himself, purified and magnified. The biblical context shows that glory can be worldly (clothing, social prestige) or spiritual (the action of God, the holiness of the Church).
G1741.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader that what appears glorious in the eyes of the world — wealth, social honor, prestige — is not necessarily so in the eyes of God. Conversely, true spiritual glory — that of the pure and holy Church in Christ — infinitely surpasses the splendor of earthly things. It is an invitation to discern where true splendor resides: not in what shines outwardly, but in the transformation that God works.

sens: Clothing worn on the body
Outward appearance that conceals or misleads about the true nature
Visible aspect of a person or thing
G1742.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes a garment, clothing in a concrete and everyday sense: it is what one wears to cover and protect oneself. John the Baptist "had a garment of camel's hair" (Matthew 3:4), which shows his austere life in the desert.

2. The garment can also refer to what covers or conceals: in the parable of the false prophets, they "come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly they are ravenous wolves" (Matthew 7:15). The sheep's clothing is a facade, a deceptive appearance that hides a dangerous reality.

3. The garment holds symbolic importance in solemn narratives: in the parable of the wedding feast, the man who has not put on a "wedding garment" commits a grave offense (Matthew 22:11-12). The appropriate garment for the context signifies respect and preparation.
G1742.origine: The Greek word enduma comes from the root enduo, which means "to put on" or "to clothe oneself." It literally denotes what envelops and covers the body. In ancient Hebrew, the word used was levush (לְבוּשׁ) which has the same concrete meaning. The family of enduma also includes verbs meaning "to dress" or "to clothe oneself."
G1742.emploi: This word appears 8 times in the New Testament, mainly in Matthew (6 occurrences) and once each in Luke and in the resurrection narrative in Matthew 28. It is used first in the literal sense: the clothing of John the Baptist reveals his renunciation of comfort (Matthew 3:4). It is also central in Jesus' teaching on worry: "Do not worry about your body, what you will wear" (Matthew 6:25, 28) where the garment symbolizes material needs. In the parables, the word takes on a moral and symbolic dimension: the sheep's clothing hides a wolf's heart (Matthew 7:15), and the wedding garment expresses the respect due to sacred events (Matthew 22:11-12).
G1742.portee: This word reminds us that outward appearance does not always reflect inner reality. Jesus warns us against those who use false appearances to deceive (Matthew 7:15). He also teaches us not to worry excessively about clothing and material needs, for God knows our necessities (Matthew 6:25). The appropriate garment also becomes a sign of respect toward God and His calls: to be spiritually "dressed correctly" is to be prepared to meet the Lord.

sens: To make strong or powerful, to give physical or moral strength to someone
To become strong, to grow in power or assurance
To become firm in faith or in a religious conviction
To be strengthened by an external cause (God, grace, faith)
G1743.detail:
1. To fortify someone means to give them strength or courage to accomplish what they undertake. Saul in Damascus becomes increasingly powerful in his arguments, "fortified" by his new faith (Acts 9:22). Paul tells Timothy: "be strong in grace" (2 Timothy 2:1), meaning draw from the grace of Jesus the strength to move forward.
2. The word also denotes an inner effect: Abraham was "fortified" by faith, meaning his trust in God grew and strengthened him despite obstacles (Romans 4:20). Paul proclaims, "I can do all things through Him who strengthens me," expressing how the power of Christ becomes his own (Philippians 4:13).
3. To fortify can also mean to "become firm," to gain solidity. It is a call to strengthen oneself, as in Ephesians 6:10: "be strong in the Lord," where the believer is invited to draw from the Lord's power to stand against spiritual battles.
G1743.origine: The Greek word is composed of ἐν (en, in) and δυνάμις (dynamis, power, strength). The image is one of a force entering someone to fill them and make them capable. In Hebrew, it translates verbs like לָבַשׁ (labash, "to clothe" with power, as one puts on a garment) and עָזַז (azazz, "to be strong"), showing that strength is not an innate quality, but something that clothes or overwhelms us.
G1743.emploi: The verb appears 7 times in the New Testament, mostly in the Pauline letters. Paul uses it to speak of his own experience: Christ "strengthened" him to preach the Gospel to the Gentiles (1 Timothy 1:12) and "strengthened" him when he preached in Rome (2 Timothy 4:17). He also describes how faith "fortifies" Abraham, or how the believer must "fortify" themselves in Christ in the face of trials. The meaning remains constant: it is always about a power that strengthens, whether it comes from God or is rooted in faith.
G1743.portee: This word reminds us that Christian strength is not that of the world or of self-will, but that which God gives to those who believe. It invites the reader not to rely on their own resources, but to "fortify" themselves daily in their relationship with God and to receive the power of Christ to live out their faith and overcome difficulties.

sens: to enter a place stealthily
to enter with a hidden or malicious intent
to gradually insinuate oneself with someone
G1744.detail:
1. This word denotes the action of stealthily entering a place, slipping in without being seen or having permission. The image is one of discreet infiltration: in 2 Timothy 3:6, it refers to false teachers who infiltrate houses to seduce gullible women.

2. The word often carries the idea of a hidden or malicious intent: it is not just entering, but entering secretly, under a pretext, to cause harm. It is a treacherous penetration, like that of an intruder.

3. By extension, the word also suggests the action of gradually insinuating oneself with a person, slowly gaining their trust through indirect means to better deceive or exploit them.
G1744.origine: The word is composed of the prefix "en-" (in) and "dûnô" which means "to enter, to penetrate." The root evokes the idea of engulfing, disappearing inside. This type of composition (verb with prefix) is typical in Greek to express nuances of movement or action. The translation as "to introduce" in French conveys this often clandestine penetration.
G1744.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Timothy 3:6, in a context of warning against false teachers and seducers. Paul writes to Timothy to warn him of the dangers threatening the Church. These impostors "infiltrate" houses to seduce weak women. The context leaves no doubt: this is not an ordinary visit, but a surreptitious infiltration, a penetration with intent to harm. The unique use of the term in the New Testament shows that it was a very real threat to the young Churches.
G1744.portee: This word reminds us of a reality that the Church has always had to face: the presence of false teachers seeking to insinuate themselves into the communities of believers. The term urges us to vigilance: not to naively welcome every word or person, but to discern real intentions. For Paul, it is such a serious threat that it deserves an explicit warning. This invites Christians to cultivate wisdom and discernment in their spiritual relationships.

sens: the action of putting on a garment
a garment that one wears
adornment, outer attire
G1745.detail: 1. The word primarily denotes the action of dressing, putting on a garment: it is the act of slipping on a piece of clothing or ornament. 2. By extension, it also refers to the garment itself, the thing one puts on and wears on their body. 3. It can also mean the entirety of the adornment or outer attire that a person wears — their clothes considered as a whole. In 1 Peter 3:3, the apostle speaks of the "adornment of garments" (literally: the action of dressing) to exhort Christian women not to be absorbed by external appearance, but to cultivate rather a hidden beauty, that of the heart.
G1745.origine: The word comes from the verb ἐνδύω (endúô), which literally means "to put on inside": ἐν (en, in) + δύω (dúô, to put). It is of the same family as the Latin verb "induere" (to dress). The word thus concretely describes the act of slipping a garment onto oneself, hence its broader meaning of "garment" and "adornment."
G1745.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Peter 3:3, where Peter exhorts Christian women: "Let your adornment not be external..." (or more literally: "Let the ornament of your garments not be..." ). The context shows that Peter is not condemning clothing in itself, but the obsession with external appearance — elaborate braids, gold, pearls — to the detriment of the beauty of the heart. The word thus emphasizes the idea of self-promotion through appearance.
G1745.portee: This word reminds Christians, particularly women, of an important lesson: our value does not reside in our external appearance or adornments, but in our character. Cultivating inner beauty — gentleness, kindness, fear of God — is infinitely more important and lasting than bodily adornments. It is an invitation to detach our self-esteem from fashion and the opinions of others.

sens: To put a garment on oneself or on someone else
To wear a garment, a robe, or a suit
To be dressed in something in a figurative sense, that is, to adopt a quality or spiritual strength
To penetrate, to intrude
G1746.detail:
1. The primary meaning is physical: to dress someone by putting clothes on them. The father in the parable dresses his prodigal son in a beautiful robe (Luke 15:22), meaning he puts it on him to honor and welcome him back.
2. By extension, to clothe simply means to wear clothes: Jesus says that one should not wear two tunics (Mark 6:9), meaning not to put on two at once; he is speaking of what one wears.
3. The word is used in a figurative sense: to clothe oneself in righteousness means to adopt righteousness as one puts on a coat (Ephesians 4:24); to clothe oneself with the Lord Jesus Christ means to take him as the guide and protector of one's entire life (Romans 13:14). In all these cases, one "puts on oneself" a spiritual reality as one puts on clothes.
4. Rarely, the word means to penetrate or intrude: false prophets who sneak into houses (2 Timothy 3:6).
G1746.origine: The Greek word comes from ἐν ("in") and δύω ("to enter, to sink in"). The basic image is that of someone being made to enter into clothing, or sinking into it. In Hebrew, the translated word is primarily לָבַשׁ (labash), which has exactly the same meaning: to clothe or to wear garments. It is a simple and common verb used to describe the action of dressing in everyday life as well as symbolic or spiritual actions.
G1746.emploi: The verb to clothe appears 25 times in the New Testament. It is first used literally: to clothe someone in garments, to wear clothes (Luke 15:22; Mark 6:9). It is also used to describe concrete actions: soldiers clothe Jesus in a purple robe (Matthew 27:31), a possessed man is clothed in Gethsemane (Luke 8:27). But the most important usage of the word in the New Testament Bible is figurative: to clothe oneself in a quality or spiritual power means to fully adopt it and live it. Romans 13:14 says, "Put on the Lord Jesus Christ": this means making Jesus the heart of one's identity and life. Ephesians 4:24 speaks of putting on the new man; Colossians 3:12 of putting on heartfelt compassion. This image of clothing makes visible an inner change: one cannot see righteousness or love, but one puts them on like a visible coat.
G1746.portee: This word reminds the reader that spiritual life is not abstract. To clothe oneself with Christ is to "wear" him as one wears clothes, allowing him to cover and protect one's entire life. The image of clothing also indicates that our spiritual qualities become visible to others: when one puts on mercy, one shows it. It is an invitation to transform not only what one believes internally but also how one presents oneself and acts in the world.

sens: A trap secretly set to surprise someone
An ambush, a hidden wait to do harm
A plot or criminal scheme
G1747.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes a hidden wait, as when soldiers or enemies hide to strike by surprise. In Acts 23:16, Paul's nephew learns that a plot is being prepared against the apostle: men are lying in wait to attack him.
2. More broadly, it refers to a murderous plot or scheme. In Acts 25:3, the Jews ask the governor for a favor: to bring Paul back to Jerusalem. But in truth, they are preparing an ambush on the way to kill him — it is a secret and criminal plan.
3. The word can also refer to the danger itself, the hidden threat that lurks.
G1747.origine: The Greek word comes from the preposition "en" (in) and "hèdra" (seat, place where one sits). The image is that of people sitting in wait, hidden somewhere, ready to pounce. The Hebrew word it often translates is "arab," which means to set an ambush. It is an action verb, that of hunters or warriors who hide.
G1747.emploi: The word appears twice in the New Testament, exclusively in the book of Acts, in a dramatic context: the trial and imprisonment of Paul. In Acts 23:16, it is a trap set by enemies of the apostle to assassinate him discreetly. In Acts 25:3, it is the same danger, renewed a few chapters later. In both cases, the word describes a criminal strategy that hides under the appearance of official actions — an assassination attempt disguised as a prisoner transfer.
G1747.portee: This word reminds the believer that danger can come in a hidden manner and that one must remain vigilant. God's providence, which warns Paul through his nephew (Acts 23:16), shows that no ambush can escape divine protection. It is also a call to discern the true intentions behind appearances and not to naively trust those who prepare evil.

sens: To set an ambush, to wait hidden to surprise someone
To prepare a verbal trap or a ruse to ensnare someone in their words
G1748.detail:
1. The literal meaning is that of a military ambush or a trap: to position oneself secretly to surprise the enemy or a prey at the moment they pass. It is the image of a hidden and malicious wait (Acts 23:21).
2. The figurative sense, more common in the New Testament, describes the act of setting a verbal trap: preparing questions or situations intended to ensnare someone, to make them contradict themselves or to discredit them. The enemies of Jesus set traps for him by trying to surprise him in his words (Luke 11:54).
G1748.origine: The word comes from the Greek ἐνέδρα (ambush, trap): ἐν (in) + ἕδρα (seat, position). The basic image is that of remaining seated or hidden in a waiting place. In Hebrew, the verb אָרַב (frequently translated in the Greek Old Testament) also means to set an ambush or to set a trap.
G1748.emploi: This Greek verb appears twice in the New Testament, always in the sense of setting a trap or an ambush. In Luke 11:54, the scribes and Pharisees set traps for Jesus by posing tricky questions to surprise a word from him that could discredit him. In Acts 23:21, it is a true ambush: more than forty sworn men have gathered to lie in wait and assassinate the apostle Paul. In both cases, the intention is clearly hostile and premeditated.
G1748.portee: This word reveals the hidden malice that lurks for the believer. It shows how the adversaries of the truth resort to cunning and organized violence rather than honesty. For the reader, it is a call to spiritual vigilance: to recognize the traps set in the form of deceptive questions or plots, and to trust in God's wisdom and protection.

sens: To roll something around someone to cover them
To pack, wrap a body
G1750.detail:
1. The word primarily means to roll a cloth around a person to cover them. It is an action of protecting or preparing. In Mark 15:46, Joseph takes the linen cloth and wraps it around the body of Jesus — it is a gesture of respect and care for the deceased.
2. More broadly, it refers to preparing a body for burial by wrapping it in a white cloth, according to Jewish custom. The linen cloth is not tied or fastened: it is simply rolled around the body, as is often seen in ancient burials.
G1750.origine: The word is composed of the prefix ἐν- ("in, within") and the verb ειλέω ("to roll, to turn"). It literally means "to roll in." In Hebrew, the verb שׁוּט (shout) or rather לוּט (lout, "to wrap") in some ancient manuscripts describes a similar action. It is a very concrete verb, describing a manipulation of the hands.
G1750.emploi: The word appears only once in Mark 15:46, at the time of Jesus' burial. Joseph of Arimathea, who is a member of the Sanhedrin and wealthy, buys a new linen cloth and uses it to wrap the body of Jesus before placing it in his own tomb hewn from rock. It is an act of honor and piety: wrapping the dead is to respect their dignity and follow the Law. The four Gospels describe this moment with the linen cloth, but Mark chooses this specific verb to emphasize Joseph's delicate and respectful action.
G1750.portee: This act of wrapping the body of Jesus in a linen cloth shows us the authentic humanity of his death. He did not escape the realities of mortality and mourning. At the same time, this linen cloth could not hold him: at the resurrection, the linen cloth remained empty. This contrast between the care taken in his burial and his glorious resurrection is a comfort for the believer in the face of death.

sens: to be inside, within
to be contained in
to be present within oneself
to be possible, feasible
G1751.detail:
1. The verb describes what exists inside a thing, what inhabits or is found there. In Luke 11:41, Jesus says, "Give as alms those things which are within," speaking of the inner content of the cup or the hearts of the Pharisees — what they possess within themselves.
2. More broadly, the word means "to be contained in" or "to be part of": it is the opposite of outside, the opposite of the visible or external.
3. By extension, it can express the idea of what is possible or achievable — what lies in some way within someone's capabilities or resources.
G1751.origine: The word is composed of the preposition ἔν ("in") and the verb εἰμί ("to be"). Literally, "to be in" or "to be inside." This preposition ἔν governs interiority, immersion, presence at the heart of something. It is a simple but fundamental word to express what is hidden, secret, or essential, as opposed to the visible or superficial.
G1751.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament in Luke 11:41, where Jesus criticizes the Pharisees who clean the outside of the cups but neglect the inside. Jesus invites them to give as alms "what is within" — in other words, to first purify their interiority, their hearts. This expression participates in the contrast that Jesus establishes in this passage between the outside (the apparent pure) and the inside (the real pure). The word emphasizes that true purity comes from what is within a person, not from external conformities.
G1751.portee: This verse invites the believer not to settle for a superficial righteousness or generosity. Giving "what is within" means giving from one's heart, from one's true resources, from one's interiority. It is a call to authenticity: true transformation of the Christian begins within and manifests outwardly, never the reverse.

sens: Indicates the reason, the motive for an action or situation
Indicates what provokes a consequence or an event
Expresses the price paid, the sacrifice made for something
Designates the person or cause for which one acts or suffers
G1752.detail:
1. Because of simply indicates why something happens or is true: it is the reason, the motive. "Blessed are those who are persecuted for righteousness' sake" (Matthew 5:10): it is because they defend righteousness that they are persecuted. The word shows the cause-and-effect relationship.

2. It also designates what triggers a consequence: it is the starting point that produces the result. "Whoever loses his life for my sake will find it" (Matthew 10:39): losing one's life produces the result of finding it, but what causes this loss is the connection with Jesus.

3. It expresses what one sacrifices or pays for a cause: "Anyone who has left houses, or brothers, or sisters, or father... for my name's sake will receive a hundredfold" (Matthew 19:29). One renounces these ties out of love for Christ.

4. It designates the person or ideal for which one acts or suffers: "They will persecute you for my name's sake" (Luke 21:12) means "for being my disciples" or "because you belong to me." It is in the name of this relationship that one endures.
G1752.origine: This Greek word comes from a root that originally expressed the idea of "end" or "purpose," then "reason" or "motive." It is composed of elements that reinforce this notion of causality. The word has variants depending on its position in the sentence (ἕνεκα or ἕνεκεν), but they retain the same meaning. The preposition always takes the genitive (the case of what follows), which reinforces the link of dependence.
G1752.emploi: This word appears 23 times in the New Testament, especially in Matthew, Mark, and Luke, in the Gospel narratives. It is particularly frequent when speaking of the persecution of the disciples: "for my name's sake," "for the good news." Paul also uses it to express causal relationships in his letters (Romans 8:36, 2 Corinthians 3:10, 7:12). The meaning remains constant: it is always about giving the reason or the motive. But depending on the context, this reason can be an idea (righteousness, the Gospel), a person (Jesus, a king), or an event. The word helps to understand why the disciples suffer: it is never by chance, but always "because of" Jesus or the Gospel.
G1752.portee: This word shows that the persecution of the disciples is not absurd or accidental: it has a cause, and that cause is Jesus himself and his Word. For the Christian, this liberates and gives courage: if I suffer "because of" the name of Christ, my suffering has meaning and nobility. It unites me to Jesus and to the Gospel, not to my own mistakes. It also helps to discern: what we renounce or for what we suffer reveals where our heart is. "Because of my name" reminds us that following Jesus has a cost, but that cost is never in vain.

sens: Force in action, capable of producing effects
Effectiveness of an action, its power to accomplish
Divine power that works and transforms
Power of Satan that manifests through wonders
G1753.detail:
1. The word denotes a force that is not inert: it is a power that acts, that unfolds concretely. Unlike a simple capacity or possibility, energeia is a force in motion, effective and operative. In Colossians 1:29, Paul says he struggles "with all his energy" — that of Christ — which works powerfully in him: it is not a dormant power, but a power that works.
2. Effectiveness refers to the result of this action: it is the power employed to accomplish something. In Ephesians 3:7, Paul received the ministry "by the effective working of His power" — that is, by the active power of God that enables him for his work.
3. Applied to God, this power is the supernatural force that transforms, resurrects, and builds up. In Colossians 2:12, believers are "raised with Him through faith in the working of God" — a power that conquers death itself. In Ephesians 1:19, Paul prays that believers may know "the exceeding greatness of His power," which worked in Christ.
4. The same power also operates through Satan: in 2 Thessalonians 2:9, the coming of the lawless one will be "according to the working of Satan, with all power, signs, and lying wonders." Even evil can claim to have operative power, but it is deceptive.
G1753.origine: The word comes from the adjective energês ("active, operative"), which is derived from the root ergia ("action, work"). It is the power that is in the process of acting, as opposed to a simple capacity or potentiality. The family of this word includes the verb energeô ("to act, to operate"), which is also found in the New Testament. The concept contrasts actual power (energeia) with potential power (dynamis): God not only has power, He exercises it.
G1753.emploi: The word energeia appears 8 times in the Greek New Testament, concentrated mainly in Paul's epistles. In Ephesians, it almost always refers to divine power: that which acts in the Church (Eph. 4:16), that which raised Christ and works on behalf of believers (Eph. 1:19, 3:7). In Colossians, it evokes the power of Christ that works in us during our spiritual resurrection (Col. 2:12) and that which strengthens us in ministry (Col. 1:29). In 2 Thessalonians, Paul uses it to describe both the false power of Satan and the lawless one (2 Th. 2:9, 2:11). Everywhere, the word denotes a power that produces concrete and visible effects, never a simple theory or a latent force.
G1753.portee: For the believer, this word reveals that God does not remain inactive: His power constantly works in the Church, in the life of every Christian, and it is the source of our spiritual resurrection and growth. Knowing this working power means learning to trust it daily, in the challenges and battles of serving God. It also frees the Christian from the fear of lies and false power: in the face of deceptive manifestations of evil, he can stand firm, assured that only the power of God produces true transformation.

sens: To function, to be in action, to produce an effect
To exercise a power, a force
To act in someone or through someone
To accomplish, to realize, to do something
G1754.detail:
1. The verb first describes the simple action of functioning or operating: a power that acts, a miracle that happens through someone. In Matthew 14:2, miracles are "done" (that is, they become real, take effect) by Jesus: the word emphasizes that something is truly at work, not just contemplated.
2. It then denotes the exercise of a power or force: a force "acts" in you, a spirit "acts" in men. Ephesians 2:2 is a striking example: the spirit of rebellion "works" in the sons of disobedience, meaning it animates, drives, governs them.
3. The word takes on a more intimate shade when it means being at work in someone, penetrating them with its action: the grace of God "works" in us (Colossians 1:29), a "working" faith of love transforms the one who possesses it (Galatians 5:6).
4. Finally, it can simply mean to accomplish, to realize: God "works" all in all (1 Corinthians 12:6), He "carries out" His purposes according to His will (Ephesians 1:11).
G1754.origine: The word comes from the root *energos*, composed of *en* ("in, within") and *ergon* ("work, labor"): it literally designates one who is in action, who works. It is the opposite of being inactive or idle. In Hebrew, it often translates the verb *paal* ("to do, to act") and *avodah* ("work, service"), which also evoke real, concrete, effective action.
G1754.emploi: The verb appears 19 times in the New Testament, mainly in Paul's epistles. It always denotes a real and effective action — never a simple project or intention. In the Gospel (Matthew 14:2, Mark 6:14), it speaks of miracles as a power that operates. In the epistles, Paul uses it to express how God or His Spirit acts in believers and in the Church: it is God who "works" all (1 Corinthians 12:6, Ephesians 1:11), His grace "works" powerfully in us (Colossians 1:29). The word also describes contrary powers: sin that "works" in us (Romans 7:5), the spirit of rebellion that "works" in the world (Ephesians 2:2). Sometimes it qualifies faith itself: a "working" faith through love (Galatians 5:6).
G1754.portee: This word speaks to the heart of the believer who wants to know if God is truly at work in him. Energéo reminds us that faith is not a passive opinion or a vague feeling: it is a real power that acts, transforms, produces concrete effects — a faith that "works" through love changes lives. It is also a warning: if a power can act in us for good (grace, the Spirit), other powers can also act for evil (sin, rebellious spirits). Finally, this verb assures us that God is never inactive: He "works" in the Church, and we are invited to collaborate with His power at work.

sens: Action of producing an effect, implementing a power
Miraculous or supernatural manifestation
Spiritual gift that manifests God's power in the Church
G1755.detail:
1. An operation is the action of making something function, implementing a force or power to produce a result. It is the act of actively engaging: God "works all in all" (1 Corinthians 12:6), meaning He deploys His power in all believers and in all areas.
2. An operation can be a miraculous or supernatural act, a visible divine intervention. Paul mentions "the gift of working miracles" (1 Corinthians 12:10): it is the ability given by the Spirit to manifest divine power through extraordinary acts.
3. In the context of spiritual gifts, an operation is a concrete manifestation of God's power within the Church. It refers to the diversity of ways God acts through His disciples: some receive one gift, others another (1 Corinthians 12:6, 10).
G1755.origine: The word comes from the verb ἐνεργέω (energéô), which means "to be active, to act, to produce an effect." Its root evokes the idea of energy, of force put into action. The word family includes terms related to activity, work, and deployed power. In Hebrew, this verb often corresponds to words denoting God's action, His hand at work, or His power in operation.
G1755.emploi: The word ἐνέργημα appears only twice in the New Testament, exclusively in 1 Corinthians 12, where Paul explains spiritual gifts. In verse 6, he refers to the diversity of operations produced by the same God. In verse 10, he cites "the gift of working miracles" as one of the particular charisms distributed by the Holy Spirit. In both passages, the word always denotes a manifestation or a concrete expression of divine power in the life of the Church.
G1755.portee: This word reminds the believer that God is not a distant or inactive God: He is the one who acts, who operates, who manifests His power. Recognizing God's operations means learning to see His hand at work in our lives and in the Church. For the Christian who receives a spiritual gift, understanding that it is an operation of God invites humility and gratitude, rather than personal pride.

sens: that produces an effect, that functions, that acts
that bears fruit, that succeeds
that has power, force of action
G1756.detail:
1. The word first describes something that is at work, actively functioning and producing concrete results. When Paul says that a "great and effective door" has opened (1 Corinthians 16:9), he speaks of a door that truly functions, that offers a real passage and opportunities for preaching. It is the image of something that works, that is not blocked or useless.
2. The word also means what bears fruit and succeeds in its purpose. The participation in the faith of Philemon must be "effective for the cause of Christ" (Philemon 1:6): it must truly produce good and serve a purpose, not remain barren. It is a call to a faith that acts and changes things.
3. Finally, it designates the word of God which is "living and effective" (Hebrews 4:12), endowed with a penetrating and powerful force that reaches the depths of the heart and judges the thoughts. Here, "effective" emphasizes the divine energy that operates through the word: it is not dead or without effect; it truly works in the one who listens to it.
G1756.origine: The word comes from Greek and literally designates what is "in energy," "in action" — hence its direct etymological link with the French word "énergie." It is built on a root that expresses the idea of working, operating, being active. The form used here (ἐνεργής) is a later variant of ἐνεργός. The underlying notion is always that of a force or capacity put into action, in movement, that truly produces something and does not remain inactive.
G1756.emploi: The word appears three times in the New Testament, always in contexts where it measures the real impact and scope of an action or a word. In 1 Corinthians 16:9, Paul uses it to describe an open missionary door: not only open, but effective, meaning truly usable and full of opportunities. In Philemon 1:6, he qualifies participation in faith, emphasizing that true participation must bear fruit and serve the cause of Christ. In Hebrews 4:12, it characterizes the word of God itself: this word is not simply written or spoken; it actively operates in the heart of the one who listens, judging their thoughts. In all cases, the word emphasizes the transition from potentiality to action, from intention to concrete effect.
G1756.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us that faith is only true if it produces fruit and manifests in real life — an "effective" faith is a faith that acts. It also invites us to recognize that the word of God is not a dead or ineffective word: it truly penetrates, judges, and transforms the one who receives it. It is a living word that operates in the secret of the heart and deserves our serious attention.

sens: to receive a blessing, to be the object of a blessing
to be declared happy and favored by God
G1757.detail:
1. This verb means to receive a blessing, that is, to be the object of God's favor and protection. In Acts 3:25, Peter reminds the Jews of the ancient promise: "All the families of the earth will be blessed in your offspring" — every nation will receive the promised blessings through Abraham's descendants.
2. The word also expresses the idea of being declared happy and favored: it is the certainty that God looks favorably and grants His grace. In Galatians 3:8, Paul shows that this blessing extends to all peoples: "All nations will be blessed in you," a promise given long before the law, by faith alone.
G1757.origine: The verb is composed of a prefix "en-" (which marks entry or state) and the verb "to bless," which comes from a root meaning "to speak well of" or "to praise." In Hebrew, it is the verb "to bless" (בָּרַךְ, barak) that the Septuagint translates by this word. The blessing is primarily a word spoken by God or by one who has authority; it then becomes the reality of the favor received.
G1757.emploi: This verb appears only twice in the Greek New Testament, in the two key passages where the Apostle Paul and Peter cite or recall the promise made to Abraham. In Acts 3:25, it is Peter who mentions this blessing in his speech to the people. In Galatians 3:8, it is Paul who emphasizes that this blessing was intended for the nations long before the coming of the Law, and that it was fulfilled by faith. In both cases, the verb underscores that the divine promise extends beyond the Jews alone: it embraces all peoples.
G1757.portee: This word reminds the Christian that he receives God's blessing only through faith, like Abraham. The original promise was intended for all peoples and all ages: it is fulfilled in the one who believes, regardless of the Law or physical descent. It is a call to trust in God's word and to the certainty that His favor extends to anyone who believes it.

sens: To hold captive, keep imprisoned
To be caught, immobilized in something like a trap
To harass someone relentlessly
To maintain under domination, a yoke
G1758.detail:
1. The primary meaning is physical: to forcibly hold someone or something, to keep them imprisoned. It is like being locked in one's hands.
2. In the passive form, the word describes the state of one who is held, stuck, unable to escape. In Galatians 5:1, Paul uses this verb to say that the Galatians risk being "held" under the yoke of slavery, "brought again under the yoke of bondage": they would be trapped by rules and legal observances.
3. The word takes on a hostile tone when it means to harass someone, to pursue them with hostility. Herodias was "angry" (literally: held by hostility) against John the Baptist: she held him in her grudge and wanted him dead (Mark 6:19).
4. Finally, to press someone means to harass them, to bombard them with questions or accusations. The scribes and Pharisees began to "press" him violently (Luke 11:53): they held him in a flood of hostile interrogations, like prisoners of the desire to trap him.
G1758.origine: The verb combines the preposition ἐν ("in, within") and ἔχω ("to have, to hold"), hence the basic image: "to hold in, to keep inside." The same root ἔχω appears in words like ἐχθρός (enemy: one who holds you against him) and in compound words where it expresses retention or opposition. In Hebrew, the verb סתם (cited in Genesis 49:23 for Greek translators) also means to enclose, to block, to retain.
G1758.emploi: The verb appears only three times in the New Testament, and each time in a tense context. In Mark 6:19, Herodias is "angry": she holds John the Baptist in her murderous rage. In Luke 11:53, the religious leaders "press" Jesus: they harass him, bombarding him with questions to trap him. In Galatians 5:1, Paul warns Christians not to be "held" under the yoke: he uses the verb in the passive to express the risk of spiritual captivity, a return to legal servitude. The word thus oscillates between hostility (Mark, Luke) and oppressive domination (Galatians).
G1758.portee: This verb reminds us that Christ has set us free. In Galatians, Paul invites us to stand firm in this freedom and not to let ourselves be "held" again by legal chains or doctrines that would imprison us. It also speaks of the harassment that the disciples endured: Jesus endured the hostile "pressing" of adversaries, and this image shows the price of our redemption. The word invites the Christian to recognize any form of captivity—spiritual, emotional, or moral—and to stand firm in the freedom found in Christ.

sens: in this place, at this location
toward this place, coming to this location
G1759.detail:
1. In this place, at this location: the word designates a place where one is or where something happens. When Jesus asks the disciples, "Do you have anything to eat here?" (Luke 24:41), he is speaking of the place where he is with them. Similarly, when the apostles are arrested in Jerusalem, it is said that "these men who have turned the world upside down have come here also" (Acts 17:6): it is in the city, at this specific place, that they are accused of causing trouble.
2. Toward this place, coming to this location: the word also indicates movement toward a place, the action of coming somewhere. The Samaritan woman says to Jesus: "so that I will no longer come here to draw" (John 4:15)—she is speaking of not coming to this well anymore. When Paul cries out in prison, "we are all here" (Acts 16:28), he means that all the prisoners and he are present, remaining in this place, not having fled.
G1759.origine: The word comes from an ancient root meaning "in this place." It is a locative adverb formed on a demonstrative base (like our "-ci" in French). It has no direct Hebrew equivalent in the Old Testament, as this word appears only in Greek in the New Testament; but it belongs to the family of common locative adverbs in classical Greek to speak of location and movement.
G1759.emploi: The word appears 8 times in the New Testament, mostly in the Gospel of John and in Acts. It is used very naturally to indicate where one is: when the resurrected Jesus asks if his disciples have food (Luke 24:41), or when someone comes to knock at Peter's door (Acts 10:18). It also serves to situate an event in a place: the accusations against the apostles "here" in Jerusalem, or Paul's trial before the governor (Acts 25:24). Its meaning varies little: it always conveys the concrete idea of presence or location.
G1759.portee: This little word reminds us that the message of Christ was incarnated in real places, concrete situations, where men and women lived. When the disciples eat with the resurrected Jesus, when Peter receives the vision at home, when Paul preaches in the cities—all of this "here," in these concrete places. This shows that the Christian faith is not an abstract theory, but a meeting that takes place on earth, in our daily reality.

sens: To reflect inwardly on something, to pose a question
To carry a thought or concern in one's mind
To form an opinion or judgment within oneself
G1760.detail:
1. The word designates the act of reflecting, of turning something over in one's mind: when Joseph "thinks" about the problem posed by Mary's pregnancy, he weighs the situation internally before making a decision (Matthew 1:20).
2. It can also refer to the thoughts or concerns that occupy the mind, particularly bad thoughts: Jesus reproaches the scribes for having evil thoughts in their hearts, meaning hidden and malicious intentions (Matthew 9:4).
3. In both cases, the word emphasizes an inner movement of the soul, what one ruminates silently within oneself before it manifests outwardly.
G1760.origine: The Greek word comes from "thymos" (the heart, the spirit, the soul) and the prefix "en-" (within), hence literally "to have something in one's mind." It denotes a movement of thought that unfolds internally, in the innermost being of the person. The Hebrew Bible uses a similar verb to mean "to imagine" or "to conceive a plan."
G1760.emploi: The verb appears twice in Matthew. In Matthew 1:20, it describes Joseph who reflects alone, probably with anxiety, on the delicate situation of his pregnant fiancée; it is in this moment of inner reflection that the angel appears to him. In Matthew 9:4, Jesus uses the same verb to refer to the malicious thoughts of the scribes, which shows his ability to discern what is hidden in the human heart even before it is spoken. The word always emphasizes a hidden mental activity, an inner work of the soul.
G1760.portee: This word invites the reader to become aware of the importance of their secret thoughts: they are never truly hidden, for Jesus sees them. It also reminds us that God intervenes in our moments of inner reflection, as he did with Joseph in a dream. It is a call to pay attention to the quality of our thoughts, beyond what we show outwardly.

sens: What occupies the mind, a reflection or intention
A feeling, a disposition of the heart
A conception of the mind, what one imagines or creates
G1761.detail:
1. What occupies the mind at the moment: a thought, a reflection, or a hidden intention. Jesus knows the thoughts of the disciples who doubt or wonder who is the greatest (Matthew 9:4 and 12:25) — not by guessing, but by reading hearts. It is something intimate that no one can hide.
2. A feeling or inclination of the heart, rather than a pure operation of reason. The word of God judges "the thoughts and intentions of the heart" (Hebrews 4:12): it reaches even the most secret movements of the soul, the true intentions.
3. What one imagines, conceives, or creates: human art and industry (Acts 17:29). These are thoughts put into action, creations of the mind.
G1761.origine: The word comes from the verb « enthuméomaï » (to reflect, to meditate): it primarily denotes the action of thinking, turning something over in one's mind (« en » = inside, « thumos » = the heart, the soul). It opposes « ennoia » (purely rational thought): the thought-feeling, which comes from the heart as much as from reason, inclinations and intuitions.
G1761.emploi: The word appears four times in the New Testament, always in the singular or plural with the meaning of what occupies the heart and mind. In Matthew (9:4 and 12:25), it designates the intimate thoughts of the disciples that Jesus discerns — intentions or doubts. In Hebrews 4:12, the word penetrates to the secret thoughts and feelings: it is the intimacy of the conscience. In Acts 17:29, the word takes on a more concrete hue: thoughts brought to form, the work of man. Each time, it concerns what remains hidden or intimate, unless someone — God or His Christ — brings it to light.
G1761.portee: This word reminds us that our most secret thoughts, our true feelings, and our hidden intentions are never unknown to God. Jesus sees what no one else can see; the divine word scrutinizes the heart. It is both a warning (nothing is hidden from God) and a comfort (He knows even what we do not know about ourselves, and loves us nonetheless).

sens: To exist, to be located somewhere
To be present in a whole, a group
To have one's place, one's role in a given context
G1762.detail:
1. The verb ἔνι expresses the existence or presence of something in a given place or moment — it simply means to be there, to have reality. In 1 Corinthians 6:5, Paul asks if there is "among you a wise man": he is asking if that man exists, if he is present in the community.

2. More specifically, the word means to have a place or role within a group or structure. In Galatians 3:28, "there is neither male nor female": this means that these distinctions have no place in the status of being a member of God's people. Similarly, in Colossians 3:11, "there is neither Greek nor Jew": these social and religious categories do not define who we are in Christ.

3. By extension, the verb can also express the idea that a quality or reality is present in someone or something. In James 1:17, "every good gift" comes from God: goodness is present in God as its source.
G1762.origine: ἔνι is an ancient Ionic form of the verb ἐνί (lit. "to be in"), reinforced by the accent. It comes from the root ἐν ("in") combined with a verbal radical. It is essentially an archaic variant of the verb ἔνεστι ("it is in, it exists"), very close to εἰμί ("to be"). This form belongs to ancient and classical Greek, and it has been preserved in the Greek of the New Testament, particularly in passages where one wants to express not only simple existence but existence within a framework, a relationship, or a specific context.
G1762.emploi: ἔνι appears 4 times in the New Testament, always in important theological contexts. In 1 Corinthians 6:5, Paul uses it to question the absence of wisdom in the Church. In Galatians 3:28, the verb appears three times to affirm that certain human categories (male/female, slave/free, Greek/Jew) have no significance for spiritual status: they have no "place" in the renewal brought about in Christ. In Colossians 3:11, the same motif reappears: these distinctions do not prevail in the new humanity. In James 1:17, the verb expresses that God is the source of all good, without change or variation — goodness has its place in Him absolutely. In all these cases, the word conveys the idea of active presence or absence of place, never neutral, but always with a spiritual or moral stake.
G1762.portee: This word invites the reader to see that our identity and place in Christ transcend the social, ethnic, or sexual categories that divide the world. It reminds us that God alone is the constant and unshakeable source of good, and that it is in Him that we find our true status, not in our earthly roles. It is a word of radical freedom and equality grounded in faith.

sens: A period of a complete revolution of the sun, twelve months
A period marked by a particular event or charge
The cyclical fulfillment of a task or rite
G1763.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes the natural duration of twelve months. In Antioch, Paul and Barnabas spent a whole year together, teaching the disciples (Acts 11:26). It is the ordinary measure of time that we all know.
2. It can also qualify a particular year, the year when something memorable occurred — for example, "that year," the year when Caiaphas was high priest and prophesied about the death of Jesus (John 11:51). The year thus bears the imprint of what happens in it.
3. In Israelite worship, the year designates the annual cycle of the rite: each year, the high priest enters the sanctuary on the Day of Atonement to offer blood (Hebrews 9:25), and each year the remembrance of sins is renewed through sacrifices (Hebrews 10:3). The year then becomes the regular rhythm by which the relationship between God and His people is renewed.
G1763.origine: The Greek eniautos comes from a root meaning "to turn in a circle," the idea of a loop or revolution. The word thus evokes the movement of the sun returning to its starting point. In the Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament), it regularly translates the Hebrew shana, which also carries the meaning of change and renewal. It is a precise word for measuring the passing of time.
G1763.emploi: The word appears fourteen times in the New Testament, mostly in Paul and in the Epistle to the Hebrews. It is used to count durations ("a year" in Antioch, Acts 11:26; "eighteen years" in Corinth, Acts 18:11) and to describe the cycles of Mosaic worship. In Hebrews, where it appears often, it reinforces the idea that Levitical rites are repeated without ever completely removing sins — year after year, blood is offered again. In Galatians 4:10, Paul reproaches the Galatians for observing days, months, and years as if these divisions of time had spiritual virtue. Luke also uses it for the "year of the Lord's favor" (Luke 4:19), borrowing the language of the jubilee; it is no longer just a duration, but a decisive moment of salvation.
G1763.portee: Thinking about the year means being aware that time passes, that each year brings its share of blessings and challenges, and that God governs this movement. For the believer, the year is not an abstraction: it is the concrete framework of daily faithfulness and prayer. In Hebrews, understanding that sacrifices are repeated each year helps to grasp that only the sacrifice of Jesus, offered once, could truly purify and liberate — there is no longer an endless cycle.

sens: to be located there, next to someone or something
to be current, ongoing, existing now
to threaten, to be imminent, to approach in a troubling manner
G1764.detail:
1. To be present or nearby means to be in a place, to exist currently. This is the simplest idea: something or someone is there, available. In 1 Corinthians 3:22, Paul speaks of the "present things" — everything that currently exists in the world of his readers.

2. To be current means to belong to the present moment, to the time in which one lives. The "difficult times" of 2 Timothy 3:1 and 1 Corinthians 7:26 are not distant catastrophes: they are realities of Paul's time, hard circumstances weighing on the Church.

3. To threaten or be imminent means to approach in a way that is concerning, weighing on the present — what is happening and will happen with urgency. In 2 Thessalonians 2:2, Paul fears that his readers believe that "the day of the Lord has already come": he uses this word to express this dreaded presence, as if the final judgment were immediately at the threshold.
G1764.origine: This word is composed of "en" (in, at) and "istēmi" (to stand, to place). The basic image is that of placing oneself inside, being set in a situation. In ancient Greek, depending on the tense used, the word acquires different meanings: the perfect and pluperfect retain the idea of a persistent state ("to be present"), while the aorist emphasizes sudden arrival ("to stand before"). In the Greek translations of the Old Testament, it often translates Hebrew verbs meaning "to stand" or "to exist."
G1764.emploi: This verb appears 7 times in the New Testament, mostly in the Pauline epistles. Paul uses it to speak of current realities and threats facing his communities. In Romans 8:38 and 1 Corinthians 3:22, he lists the "present things" among the powers that nothing can separate the believer from the love of Christ. In 1 Corinthians 7:26 and 2 Timothy 3:1, the "difficult times" refer to the current sufferings and trials of the Church. In Galatians 1:4, the "present evil age" contrasts with the world to come. In 2 Thessalonians 2:2, the idea that "the day of the Lord has already come" expresses a false doctrine: that day is not yet present despite what some claim. The word thus nuances between simple presence and threatening imminence.
G1764.portee: This word reminds the believer that God sees not only the visible and current realities but that He dominates all dimensions of them. When Paul says that nothing — neither present things nor things to come — can separate us from the love of Christ, he assures us that our faith is not fragile in the face of circumstances. It is also a warning: recognizing the "difficult times" of the present helps the believer to remain vigilant and not to be deceived by false promises about the imminence of the end.

sens: to give physical strength to someone, to make them vigorous
to regain strength, to recover energy after a weakening
to affirm, to support someone in a spiritual or moral trial
G1765.detail:
1. The primary meaning is physical: to give strength or vigor to the body. It is to restore someone who is exhausted or weakened, as when Saul "after he had taken food, regained his strength" (Acts 9:19) — he regains body and health.

2. The word also carries a spiritual and moral dimension: to strengthen can mean to support, to encourage someone in the midst of a struggle or suffering. When an angel "appeared from heaven to strengthen him" in Luke 22:43, it is about giving courage and inner strength to Jesus in his agony at Gethsemane, not healing his body, but affirming his spirit.
G1765.origine: The word is composed of the prefix ἐν- ("in, into") and ἰσχύς ("strength, power"). The image is that of putting strength into someone, filling them with power. The Greek translates the Hebrew חָזַק (hazaq), which literally means "to be strong, to strengthen." It is a word of divine action: God strengthens the weak and the discouraged.
G1765.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the New Testament. In Luke 22:43, the agonizing Jesus receives heavenly reinforcement from an angel, in the context of his intense prayer at Gethsemane. In Acts 9:19, after his conversion and blindness, Saul regains his physical strength by eating, an image of his complete restoration. In both cases, the word describes a turnaround: from weak to strong, from discouraged to supported. It is always an action that restores or supports the one in distress.
G1765.portee: This word reminds us that true strength — whether physical or spiritual — does not primarily come from ourselves, but from the help that God provides to His children. It can come through the Spirit, through a word, through an angel, or through the simple means of life (food, rest). It is a word of hope for those who feel exhausted or discouraged in faith.

sens: the number 9 in a series
the ninth hour of the day (three o'clock in the afternoon)
G1766.detail:
1. Ninth means the number that comes after the eighth in a succession. It is the ordinal adjective that indicates this position. The text of Revelation 21:20 uses it to describe a precious stone in the order of the foundational stones of the heavenly Jerusalem.
2. In the Gospels, the ninth hour refers to three o'clock in the afternoon according to the Jewish day count that begins at sunrise. Matthew 27:45-46 recounts that darkness covered the earth from the sixth to the ninth hour, and it is at this ninth hour that Jesus cried out his last words on the cross: "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" This precise moment marks the climax of the Passion drama. Similarly, in Acts 3:1, it is at the ninth hour that a lame beggar is carried to the Beautiful Gate of the temple, just before his healing miracle.
G1766.origine: The Greek word ennatos comes from the root of the number nine (ennéa). It is an ordinal adjective that ranks things: first, second, third… up to ninth. In Acts 10:3 and 10:30, it designates the precise hour when Cornelius receives the vision of the angel, showing how the Greeks who read the Bible adopted this system of enumerating hours to speak of time.
G1766.emploi: The word appears ten times in the New Testament, concentrated mostly in the Gospels and Acts. It is used twice for the order of a thing (Revelation 21:20 for the ninth stone), but the other eight times it specifically designates the ninth hour of the day. This hour often coincides with significant spiritual events: the three dark hours of Christ's crucifixion (Matthew, Mark, Luke), but also moments of prayer at the temple (Acts 3:1) or divine vision (Acts 10:3, 10:30). The ninth hour seems to be a significant moment in the spiritual life of Israel.
G1766.portee: For the Christian, noting that it is at the ninth hour that Jesus dies on the cross invites reflection on this decisive moment: it is precisely at three o'clock in the afternoon that the Son of God bore our salvation. This precise timing given by the Holy Spirit in the Gospels reminds us that every detail of the Passion was intended and accomplished according to God's plan. It is a call to recognize that our redemption is not a vague event, but a fact anchored in history, at a specific day and hour.

sens: The number 9, the base digit of the decimal system
Used alone or in composed numerical expressions
G1767.detail:
1. The number nine first appears alone in the account where Jesus heals ten lepers: "Were not ten cleansed? But where are the nine?" (Luke 17:17). Here, the word simply refers to nine individuals among the ten.

2. The word takes on full significance in the parable of the Good Shepherd, where Jesus speaks of a shepherd who has one hundred sheep: "Does he not leave the ninety-nine on the mountains?" (Matthew 18:12). This number symbolizes those who have not gone astray, those who appear "righteous" and do not need repentance. The repetition of this expression in Matthew 18:13, Luke 15:4, and Luke 15:7 emphasizes the contrast between the multitude of apparent righteous and the unique importance of the one who is lost.
G1767.origine: The Greek word ennea comes from a Proto-Indo-European root that generated "nine" in English and "neuf" in French. It is a fundamental number in ancient numbering systems. In Hebrew, the number nine is said as "tisha." This word has no complex etymology: it is simply the cardinal numeral term for the digit 9.
G1767.emploi: The word "nine" (or more often "ninety-nine") appears only five times in the Gospels. Four occurrences are found in the parable of the Good Shepherd (Matthew 18:12-13 and Luke 15:4, 7), where Jesus uses it to refer to the ninety-nine sheep that the shepherd leaves to seek the one that is lost. One isolated occurrence is found in Luke 17:17, in the account of the ten healed lepers, of whom nine do not return to thank Jesus. In all cases, the number serves to highlight the numerical and moral contrast: the great majority on one side, the exception on the other.
G1767.portee: These passages teach the reader that God pays special attention to the one who strays or sins, to the point of actively seeking them. The number ninety-nine is not an approximation: it underscores the apparent absurdity of the shepherd's dedication and invites the believer to understand that God's love does not count — it is fully directed toward the one who is lost. Furthermore, the account of the ten lepers reminds us that gratitude is not automatic, even in the face of miracles: nine forget to return, only one gives thanks.

sens: the number 90
G1768.detail: 1. The number 90, composed of nine tens. This number only appears in the parables of the lost sheep: Jesus speaks of the shepherd who has one hundred sheep and loses one, leaving the ninety-nine others (Matthew 18:12). The number emphasizes the contrast here: the vast majority are not lost, but it is the one who strays that captures the shepherd's attention and joy.
G1768.origine: Greek word formed from the number nine (ἐννέα) multiplied by ten. It is a composite number that Greek expresses by placing the units before the tens. The word remains unchanged regardless of its position in the sentence (it is said to be "indeclinable").
G1768.emploi: The word appears only four times in the New Testament, all in the two parallel versions of the parable of the lost sheep: in Matthew (18:12-13) and in Luke (15:4, 7). In these two accounts, Jesus uses this number to show that the shepherd leaves the ninety-nine sheep in safety to seek the one that is lost. The number is not insignificant: it mathematically expresses that the majority are safe, but the loss of one justifies extraordinary action.
G1768.portee: This parable teaches the infinite value of each person in God's eyes. The ninety-nine righteous, seemingly numerous and safe, do not evoke as great a joy as that of the repentant sinner. The number contrasts with the uniqueness of the one who is lost, reminding the Christian that each person counts for God, and that the conversion of a single individual brings about heavenly joy (Luke 15:7).

sens: Struck with amazement and silence, unable to speak
Rendered mute by surprise or fear
G1769.detail:
1. The word describes someone who is seized with such astonishment that they lose their speech. It is a deep amazement that paralyzes: one cannot say anything. On the road to Damascus, Paul's companions "stood astonished" (Acts 9:7) — they heard a voice from heaven, saw a brilliant light, but did not know what was happening: fear and amazement had deprived them of their voice.
2. The term can also emphasize total muteness caused by fright or emotional shock. It is the silence of one who wishes to speak but cannot, so overwhelming is the event that has shaken them.
G1769.origine: The word comes from a Greek root that evokes the idea of being inside, enclosed, locked in — hence the image of someone whose speech is like locked away by emotion. This same root is found in other Greek words referring to silence or mutism. In Hebrew, there are similar terms meaning "mute" or "voiceless," notably in the Greek translation of Isaiah 56:10.
G1769.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 9:7, at the moment when Paul is struck down by the vision of the Lord on the road to Damascus. The traveling companions experience a supernatural event — they hear a mysterious voice, see a wondrous light — but do not understand what is happening to Paul. Astonishment and fear render them astonished, unable to react or say a word. It is the moment when the reality of the invisible world breaks into the visible world, and the witnesses remain mute with surprise.
G1769.portee: This word reminds us that in the face of God's acts, we are often left speechless — our reason and words fail us. The astonishment of Paul's companions shows the abyss between our human understanding and the reality of God acting. It invites us to recognize the limits of our explanations and to submit to what surpasses us.

sens: To make a gesture with the head or hand to communicate with someone
To express something without speaking, through a movement of the body
G1770.detail:
1. To make a gesture with the head or hand to communicate with someone — it is a movement of the body that replaces speech. In Luke 1:62, when Zechariah cannot speak (he has become mute), the people "made signs" to his father to ask him a question: instead of saying words, they move their heads or hands to make themselves understood.
2. To express something without speaking, through a movement of the body — it is a means of communication when the voice is lacking or when one wants to remain discreet. The word suggests a clear intention: the one who signals wants to convey a specific message, not just attract attention.
G1770.origine: The word comes from the Greek root "neuō" which means "to make a sign with the head." The prefix "en-" adds the idea of an action directed towards someone ("in the direction of"). It is a concrete verb: it describes a bodily gesture, something that is seen and understood without hearing the voice. In the Greek Old Testament, this verb translates the Hebrew "qaratz," which means to wink or make a gesture with the lips — discreet signs of the face.
G1770.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 1:62. In this passage, Zechariah has just had a son (John the Baptist), but he has remained mute since the appearance of the angel. Neighbors and relatives come to see the newborn, and they ask Zechariah how he wants to name him — but since he cannot speak, they "make signs" to his father Zechariah to know his will. It is a moment of gestural communication, simple and effective despite the obstacle of silence.
G1770.portee: This word reminds us that God hears and understands beyond words. Zechariah, deprived of his voice, remains capable of communicating and expressing his will: God honors his intention even in silence. For us, this shows that gestures, looks, and intentions of the heart speak as strongly as words — God sees them all.

sens: Act of thinking, considering something
State of mind, intention or resolution
Inner feeling or conviction
G1771.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes the act of thinking, reflecting on something — thought as an activity of the mind. It is what happens in our heart and intellect when we consider things (Hebrews 4:12).
